description: Turn your favorite design into a unique 3D T-shirt 👕🖨️ These thin and flexible 3D prints are designed to be heat-transferred directly onto fabric using a household iron. The result is a durable and eye-catching 3D design that combines modern 3D printing technology with fashion. Instructions 🛠️👕 Download the model and open it in Bambu Studio 💻 Print the model using the recommended settings and carefully remove it from the build plate. ⚠️ Handle with care — the model is extremely thin (approximately 0.3 mm) and may tear or deform if bent too aggressively. Prepare your ironing area: Place the T-shirt on an ironing board or a flat heat-resistant surface. Set your iron to a very high temperature (almost maximum heat, without steam) 🔥 Allow the iron to fully preheat before starting. Position the printed model on the desired area of the T-shirt and cover it with baking/parchment paper 📄 Apply firm pressure with the preheated iron for 15–20 seconds. For larger designs, move the iron slowly and evenly to ensure the entire model receives sufficient heat. Maintain consistent pressure throughout the process. ⏱️ Allow the area to cool for a few seconds, then carefully remove the paper. ✅ The model should remain attached to the fabric while the paper lifts away easily. (Optional) Turn the T-shirt inside out and iron the reverse side of the applied design for an additional 5–10 seconds to improve adhesion. 👕✨ Important ⚠️ Always use the iron at a very high temperature (near maximum setting) and with the steam function turned off. Insufficient heat or pressure may result in poor adhesion to the fabric. Test on a small area first if using delicate or heat-sensitive fabrics. Care Instructions 🧼 Wash garments at temperatures not exceeding 50°C (122°F). Turn the T-shirt inside out before washing whenever possible. Avoid bleach and aggressive washing programs. Do not tumble dry at high temperatures. ⚠️ Washing or drying at excessive temperatures may cause the 3D print to loosen or peel from the fabric over time.

description: Turn your favorite design into a unique 3D T-shirt 👕🖨️ These thin and flexible 3D prints are designed to be heat-transferred directly onto fabric using a household iron. The result is a durable and eye-catching 3D design that combines modern 3D printing technology with fashion. Instructions 🛠️👕 Download the model and open it in Bambu Studio 💻 Print the model using the recommended settings and carefully remove it from the build plate. ⚠️ Handle with care — the model is extremely thin (approximately 0.3 mm) and may tear or deform if bent too aggressively. Prepare your ironing area: Place the T-shirt on an ironing board or a flat heat-resistant surface. Set your iron to a very high temperature (almost maximum heat, without steam) 🔥 Allow the iron to fully preheat before starting. Position the printed model on the desired area of the T-shirt and cover it with baking/parchment paper 📄 Apply firm pressure with the preheated iron for 15–20 seconds. For larger designs, move the iron slowly and evenly to ensure the entire model receives sufficient heat. Maintain consistent pressure throughout the process. ⏱️ Allow the area to cool for a few seconds, then carefully remove the paper. ✅ The model should remain attached to the fabric while the paper lifts away easily. (Optional) Turn the T-shirt inside out and iron the reverse side of the applied design for an additional 5–10 seconds to improve adhesion. 👕✨ Important ⚠️ Always use the iron at a very high temperature (near maximum setting) and with the steam function turned off. Insufficient heat or pressure may result in poor adhesion to the fabric. Test on a small area first if using delicate or heat-sensitive fabrics. Care Instructions 🧼 Wash garments at temperatures not exceeding 50°C (122°F). Turn the T-shirt inside out before washing whenever possible. Avoid bleach and aggressive washing programs. Do not tumble dry at high temperatures. ⚠️ Washing or drying at excessive temperatures may cause the 3D print to loosen or peel from the fabric over time.

description: Spin Your Words – Custom Text Grip Fidget Ring This is not just another fidget ring with text on it. This is a fully parametric print-in-place spinner ring where the custom text becomes the actual tactile grip of the rotating outer ring. Instead of using standard grooves, ribs or generic knurling, the external grip is generated directly from your own text, name, brand, nickname, date or message. Your text is not decoration. Your text is the grip. A Personal Message You Can Wear, Touch and Spin Because the grip is generated from custom text, this ring can become much more than a simple fidget toy. It can be a name, a romantic message, a special date, a couple nickname, an inside joke, a maker signature or a short phrase wrapped around a rotating ring. This makes it perfect as a unique personalized gift for someone special. A small object, but with a message built directly into its function. You can turn a name, a date or a love message into a tactile spinning ring. Examples: I LOVE YOU FOREVER YOU & ME MY LOVE ALWAYS LUCA ❤️ SARA SINCE 2024 SPIN MY HEART The message is not hidden inside the model. It is the part you touch, feel and spin. The Key Idea Most fidget rings use a standard external pattern for grip. This model does something different. The outer rotating ring uses raised custom text wrapped around the side surface as the tactile texture. The letters create: the grip the feel the visual identity the personalization So every ring can be different. Minimal, romantic, funny, branded, personal or completely weird: it depends only on the text you choose. Custom Text Becomes Functional Grip The text is placed on the outside of the rotating ring and follows the circular shape of the model. It is not simply stamped on a flat face. It is not just decorative branding. It becomes the surface your fingers touch while spinning the ring. Short texts are automatically repeated around the ring. Longer phrases are repeated only when they fit completely. No broken words. No interrupted messages. Only complete readable text patterns. Main Features Custom text used as tactile grip Print-in-place spinner ring Two-piece rotating structure No assembly required No external knurling Raised side text replaces the grip texture Automatic full-word text repetition No interrupted words or broken phrases Parametric inner diameter Adjustable ring width Adjustable text spacing Adjustable character width Adjustable text relief Adjustable print-in-place clearances Comfort-fit internal profile Chamfered inner edges for easier wearing Supportless design Designed for MakerWorld Customizer Multicolor-ready design Assembly and separate-part export modes What Makes It Different This model combines three things in one object: custom text + functional tactile grip + print-in-place rotating fidget ring The result is a small, simple object with a very clear identity: a personalized spinner ring where the message itself becomes the texture. It is not a ring with a label. It is a ring where the label becomes the grip. Text Ideas You can use names, brands, nicknames, short messages, romantic phrases or maker signatures. Examples: Made by CiCAdesign SPIN YOUR WORDS YOUR TEXT HERE FOCUS RELAX MAKER CREATE CUSTOM I LOVE YOU FOREVER ALWAYS YOU & ME Short words will repeat several times around the ring. Longer phrases will appear only as complete repetitions. Print-in-Place Mechanism The model is made of two separate functional parts printed together: an inner ring that stays fixed an outer ring that rotates around it Both parts rest on the build plate, making the model easier to print without supports. After printing, gently free the outer ring and rotate it gradually until the mechanism becomes smooth. Clearance parameters are available to adapt the model to different printers, materials and calibration levels. Export Modes The Customizer includes different export modes. Use: complete_assembly to generate the full print-in-place ring as one STL. Use the separate modes: inner_ring_only outer_rotating_ring_only text_grip_only to generate the three individual parts separately. The separate-part exports are useful for advanced multicolor workflows where the parts are imported together into the slicer as a single multipart object. Multicolor Printing This model can be printed in two different ways. Single Color Print For a standard single-color print, use the full assembly export and print the STL as it is. No extra steps are required. Select complete_assembly Export STL Import into slicer Print normally This is the simplest option and works like a normal print-in-place fidget ring. Multicolor Print – Single STL Workflow For the quickest multicolor workflow, export the full assembly STL and split it into parts inside Bambu Studio. Recommended workflow: 1. Select complete_assembly 2. Export STL 3. Import the STL into Bambu Studio 4. Right click on the model 5. Select Split 6. Choose Split to Parts 7. Assign a different filament/color to each part 8. Disable Arachne wall generator 9. Use Classic wall generator 10. Slice and print The model is designed to be divided into separate printable parts: inner ring outer rotating ring text grip This allows you to create 2-color or 3-color versions. Examples: outer ring: blue inner ring: light gray text grip: white or: outer ring: black inner ring: gold text grip: ivory or: outer ring: white inner ring: teal text grip: coral Multicolor Print – Separate Part Workflow For the cleanest multicolor setup, you can also export the three parts separately from the same SCAD file. Use: inner_ring_only outer_rotating_ring_only text_grip_only Then import the three generated STL files together into Bambu Studio as a single object with multiple parts. This workflow is useful if you want better control over the three colors and want the slicer to treat each component as a separate part from the beginning. In this workflow, the text grip export is positioned to bond correctly with the outer rotating ring when the parts are imported together. Important Multicolor Note When the complete assembly is split into parts, you may see very thin construction lines connecting the raised letters. These lines are intentional. They are used only to keep the custom text connected as a single selectable text-grip part inside the slicer, instead of having every letter detected as a separate object. These construction lines are necessary for multicolor part detection. They are not intended as visible design details. Do not use Arachne wall generator for multicolor printing. Use Classic wall generator instead. With Arachne enabled, the slicer may try to print these thin construction lines. With Classic wall generator, they should remain non-printable construction geometry and disappear from the final toolpath. So, when using multicolor mode: inner ring = one part outer rotating ring = one part text grip = one connected part This makes it much easier to assign colors in Bambu Studio without selecting every single letter manually. Final practical note: For single-color printing, print the complete assembly normally. For quick multicolor printing, split the complete assembly into parts and assign colors. For advanced multicolor printing, export the three parts separately and import them together as one multipart object. For multicolor printing, use Classic wall generator instead of Arachne. The thin connection lines help the slicer treat the text as one text-grip part. Comfort Fit The inner surface is shaped for better comfort. It includes: a slightly curved internal profile chamfered upper and lower inner edges smoother finger insertion improved wearing feel This makes the ring more comfortable to wear, hold and spin. Recommended Print Settings Orientation: flat on the build plate Supports: no Layer height: 0.16 – 0.20 mm Walls: 3 Top/bottom layers: 4 – 5 Infill: 15 – 25% Brim: optional For best rotation: Use a clean first layer Avoid excessive elephant foot Do not over-squish the print Free the outer ring gently after printing Rotate gradually until smooth For multicolor prints: Use Classic wall generator Do not use Arachne wall generator Customizer Parameters The model is intentionally simple to customize. Main parameters: inner diameter ring width custom side text text spacing character width text relief radial clearance axial clearance export mode The advanced geometry is already tuned, so the user can focus on the fun part: writing the text and printing a unique ring. model_name: Rubber Band Powered Toy Plane THAT FLIES
description: Description This is my second iteration of a rubber-band-powered 3D printed plane. The fuselage has been redesigned around a NACA 0012 aerofoil profile. The model also uses an adjustable flat wing. The front propeller is a 3D printed 3 blade propeller driven by a rubber band. The materials and assembly approach are pretty similar, but this version was printed using Bambu Lab PLA Matte Ivory White filament. This model is intended as a toy and a simple educational aircraft. Materials Required 3D printer duh Rubber band (40 to 50 mm) Super glue Bambu Lab PLA Matte Ivory White filament or any other suitable filament. Optional: sandpaper or small file for cleaning tight printed joints Assembly Instructions Step 1: Print all parts Print all the model parts. For best results, keep the parts lightweight. A heavy fuselage or propeller will reduce flight performance. After printing, remove any stringing, rough edges or small blobs from the parts. Step 2: Adjust the adjustable wing The wing should sit straight and level when viewed from the front. Small changes to the wing position or angle can be used later to trim the flight path. Step 3: Insert the rod hook and attach the small nub Insert the rod, as shown in the pictures, and then add the nub on the outside of the nose of the plane. Do not glue anything as off yet. Step 4: Install the propeller Then insert the propeller after the nub and glue only the front of the propeller to the rod, make sure to not glue the nub to the nose or rod. Allow the glue to dry fully before installing the rubber band or testing the propeller. Check that the propeller can rotate freely, which then inturn should also now turn the hook and thus wind the rubber band. The nub should be abe to rotate independently to the propeller and hook. If the propeller is stiff, lightly clean or sand the contact area until it spins smoothly. Step 5: Attach the rubber band Attach one end of the rubber band to the rear hook on the fuselage. Attach the other end to the propeller hook. The rubber band should sit along the fuselage centreline. It should be tight enough to drive the propeller, but not so tight that it bends the fuselage or pulls the propeller out of alignment. Step 6: Check alignment Before winding the rubber band, check the full model alignment. The fuselage should be straight, the wing should be level or adjusted, and the propeller should spin freely. The rubber band should not rub heavily against the printed body. If the model turns too much during testing, adjust the wing position slightly and test again. Step 7: First test wind Wind the propeller gently by hand for the first test. Do not fully wind the rubber band immediately. Start with a low number of turns to check that the propeller works and that the rubber band stays attached. Release the propeller carefully and check that it spins smoothly. Step 8: Flight trimming Test the plane in a clear open area. If the nose drops or rises quickly, increase throw speed or try a different wing angle. (CoG sits below the wings so the issue can be fixed with just how you throw it). If the plane rolls or turns sharply, check that the wing is symmetrically bent or is flat and that the propeller is aligned with the fuselage centreline. Notes This model is designed for simple educational testing and is a toy, not long-distance powered flight (a motorised version would be cool). Lightweight printing improves performance. The propeller must spin freely for the rubber band mechanism to work properly. The adjustable wing is useful for experimenting with stability and trim. Test indoors only if there is enough space, or outdoors in calm conditions. Do not aim the plane at people, animals, windows or fragile objects. One of the weak points of this model is the hook for the rubber band at the back of the plane. Do reinforce it with either superglue (worked best for me) or epoxy. Print Material Used Printed using Bambu Lab PLA Matte Ivory White filament.

description: This is my take on a motorized shade solution for automating existing roller-style shades. This works with traditional cordless roller shades (the spring loaded type that you pull down). Its based around a relatively cheap aliexpress geared brushless motor with an encoder driven by an esp32 for use with ESPHome and HomeAssistant. The finished product is capable of accurate positional control and uses a reed switch at the full open position to re-home the system each time the shade is fully opened. They are relatively quiet, very reliable and operate on 12v DC power. You will have to attach a small magnet to the shade (with tape or something). Here is the Bill of Materials: Item Qty Links Socket head cap M3x6 7 Socket head cap M2x4 7 Small Neodymium Magnet 1 CHR-GM25-BL2418 DC12V i34 (130rpm variant) 1 Link Alibaba (cheaper for bulk) MKA17101 Reed Switch NO 1 Link 5v Buck Converter 1 Link 3x7cm Protoboards 1 Link ESP32 1 Link 608 2RS Ball Bearing 1 Link The more of these you build the cheaper they are per unit because you end up buying the smaller components in bulk anyways. If you make 5 of them they end up being around $25 each. Use Alibaba for the motors if ordering more than one or two. In theory you probably don't need a protoboard if you really want to cut costs. There are two versions of the printed files, one with holes sized for heat-set inserts and one with holes meant to be directly threaded into. Here is a diagram of the wiring: Push the reed switch as much towards the esp32 (into the page) as possible to get it closest to the magnet that you will attach to the shade. When attaching the magnet to the shade, it works best if it is mounted sideways rather than flat. Here is a picture of how I did it, and so far it has never failed to home properly after a month of use. Wherever you place it will determine the stopping point of the shade. Magnet on back side of shade The bottom endpoint is configurable inside home assistant. The only issue I have run into is drift over many cycles if the shade isn't homed for a while (eg. 50% →0% → 50%) over and over without fully opening. This happens only when the shade travels down at full speed and abruptly stops. If you add a ramp and run it downwards at around 80% speed there will be no drift even after 20+ cycles. The YAML included has many customizable parameters related to this. Without the ramp function at the end and at full speed, after around 20 ish cycles it will drift downwards about an inch. Even still, as long as they are opened fully periodically, this will never be a problem. Assembly should be pretty straightforward if you follow the exploded view diagram. The gear shroud needs to be snapped on and might require some force, Its not meant to come off again without breaking. I've also included a version of the wall plate with different mounting points for shallower window frames and the hanger I used for the other end of the shade. You may also need to make a different size shade insert to fit in your particular tube. If you leave a comment with the inner diameter of your tube i can add more variants. That's it! Happy printing!

description: Hey everyone, long time no see! Today, I’m introducing my first Cyberbrick creation: the Cyberexcavator. Of course, including its matching remote control. I’ve been eyeing a project like this ever since Cyberbrick was first released. From the very beginning, my plan was to go big and create something truly elaborate. What was also extremely important to me was complete documentation of the entire assembly process. This project is complex and definitely surpasses many other Cyberbrick offerings in its complexity. Nevertheless, everything is explained in such detail in over 100 pages of assembly guide with countless photos, comments, tips, and more that even a dedicated beginner can attempt it! I had always set my sights on an excavator project, but it wasn't until the "Electric Push Rod for Cyberbrick" article was published by Maker Supply, that my ideas finally became feasible. I’ve spent many weeks working on this model - constantly making improvements, printing countless prototypes, going through many spools of filament, and so on. This little excavator handles small stones, sand, and the like with ease, is very precise to control, and of course, it can also pull off the occasional acrobatic maneuver. Here you can see it heading back to where it came from xD. For me, it was exactly the kind of project that’s been "almost finished" for a month and a half, simply because I kept coming up with new ideas! I didn't just want to create a model, but an entire playground - objects that can be interacted with, and so on. I'll tell you a lot more about this model later, but first we have to come to a very important part, which is probably most relevant for most people.: the hardware. To build this model, meaning ONE excavator and ONE remote control including props, you will need the "Cyberbrick Ultimate Hardware Kit ZK003", three "Electric Pushrods PG003", some additional Cyberbrick electronic components, as well as parts such as bearings and screws. To find exactly the items you need, it's best to take a close look at this list (also note the quantities, as some items are needed multiple times): Here, you need to click on „More“ to access the full list. Each thunbnail acts like a link that will guide you to the individual components/kits in the bambu lab store. The desktop version of MakerWorld even has a button that allows you to automatically add all items to your shopping cart - so you don't have to search for everything individually! I tried to keep the number of parts manageable, but this project wouldn't have been possible in this form with the standard kit. What's listed here is precisely what you need to completely recreate the project. The props, which I offer here as a separate profile, naturally don't require any hardware parts and are 100% 3D printed. Though, Not every single part from the Ultimate Hardware Kit is used. So, if you already own some Cyberbrick components, the following list will certainly be helpful to you. I have listed every single component individually here: Article Code Qty. 200mm Servo Extension Cable 3Pin (2PCS) XC011 1 BT2 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA193 1 Pack BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA112 1 Pack BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA108 2 Packs BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA201 2 Packs Micro Steel Deep Groove Ball Bearings EA004 5 Packs Wire Pair with SH1.0 IC007 1 030 Micro DC Motor with SH1.0 (2PCS) LA024 2 Packs Dual-axis Plastic Reduction Gear Kit LA017 2 100mm Wire with 2Pin XH2.54 Connectors (2PCS) XC005 2 Packs WS2812 RGB LED with IDC0.8 4PIN (2PCS) KB003 2 Packs Three-Position Rocker Switch Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector XA010 1 WS2812 LED Hub with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA006 2 14500 7.4V 800mAh Li-ion Battery (1PCS) PC003 4 Momentary Button Module with 2Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA008 2 Power Switch Module with 2Pin XH2.54 Connector (1PCS) XA007 4 Dual-Axis Joystick Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connectors (1PCS) XA011 2 Single-Axis Joystick Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA009 3 Electric Push Rod PG003 3 Remote Control Transmitter Shield (1PCS) XA005 2 Remote Control Receiver Shield (1PCS) XA004 2 Multi-Function Core Board (1PCS) XA003 4 D4x2 mm Round Magnet (20PCS) CA001 2 Packs However, if you don't own any of the parts yet , it is more cost-effective to order according to the official bill of materials that is found in this post. I’ve looked into this closely, so don't go to the trouble of recalculating it yourself :)f Now that we have discussed everything regarding the hardware, we can return to the model and what makes it special. My idea for the "Cyberexcavator" was to have two completely independently controllable sections: a tracked drive unit and a turret with an excavator arm, each equipped with its own receiver. Why? Because this eliminates the need for cables running between the two sections, allowing the turret to rotate continuously without restriction. This was quite a challenge, as I wanted to keep the model as compact as possible so the scale would align reasonably well with the electric push rods. It was difficult because I had to fit a significant amount of electronics into a very tight space. For me, it was out of the question to design a nice-looking exterior shell while the interior was a chaotic mess of cables and components; every single part has a designated spot where it is securely mounted. The exact same applies to the remote control. I originally designed the drive train with TPU tracks. These offer a bit more grip and deliver the best performance for climbing maneuvers. However, the excavator doesn't spin quite as quickly on the spot with them. The increased friction makes it harder for the tracks to slide across the surface, depending on the terrain you're driving on. For this reason—and because I know many people are hesitant to work with TPU, I also designed a PLA track. After quite a few attempts, I created a version that I personally like even better than the TPU one. It allows for very precise and relatively snappy movement. Pivoting on the spot works wonderfully, even on soft surfaces like a sofa, carpet, or similar. The video where I climb onto the A1 Mini with it, features the PLA tracks; it still works very well, though it requires a bit more finesse with the controls :) Here you can take a look at the various prototypes and part versions that were printed to ensure everything is absolutely right! I decided to set up my main print profile with the PLA tracks. You can find the TPU tracks in a separate profile. However, those require different drive sprockets—which you'll also need to print—and these are included in that profile as well. I cover this in more detail in the assembly guide! I personally really like this part—the turntable that sits between the upper and lower sections of the excavator. It is printed "in place." The outer ring has an internal thread that engages with the corresponding pinion gear on a servo later on. Although I have already noted this in the print plate labels, please do not print this part using matte or fiber-reinforced (CF/GF) filaments. This part requires a filament that produces a smooth surface! For all other parts, the choice of material is technically quite flexible. All battery compartments on this model, as well as on the remote control, are magnetic. For the excavator, the entire upper body section is simply removed, which also provides good access to other components if needed. The powertrain battery can be accessed via a small flap in the base plate, which is also designed as a print-in-place part. It’s much the same story with the remote control. Incidentally, I opted against the disposable battery cases included in the "Ultimate Hatdware Kit" and instead installed rechargeable batteries from the "Cyberbrick" range. I feel that disposable batteries have no place in applications like this in 2026, and it pays for itself very quickly in terms of cost, too. I probably spent two days working on the back section of the remote control alone. Batteries are installed on both sides, each powering a transmitter module. It, too, is printed "in place"—essentially in its closed state. This part gives the remote control an even more industrial look, which is exactly what I’m aiming for. If you have large hands, you might curse a bit here and there when plugging in the batteries—like I do—since it’s all pretty tight. But with some light and a little practice, I can manage it in two seconds now. Here are a few examples of the excavator's controls and functions: The general lighting can be adjusted to two levels and, of course, switched off completely to save battery power. To capture that authentic construction site feel, there is naturally a hazard warning light system, as well as a button that sets the front LEDs to run at full power. You only need the left stick to control the tank tracks. With a bit of finesse - which most people will surely pick up quickly, the model handles beautifully and precisely. There is the most to say about controlling the arm and the bucket, and consequently, there are the most controls for them. When pushed up or down, the right main joystick functions to retract or extend the arm as a whole. The three elements at the bottom control the individual parts of the arm independently. The clue is that identical inputs to the transmitter cancel each other out. This means, for example, that one of the arm segments can be "frozen" while operating the main joystick simply by engaging one of the small levers. Here, for instance, you can see how I achieve a fairly authentic-looking "digging motion" by combining the main stick with the small left lever. By combining the main stick and the small middle lever, for example, you can easily create a movement that allows the excavator to lift itself up. That is exactly what I do in the video when climbing onto the A1 Mini. When I play around with the unit, I hardly ever use more than two levers at a time for the arm—that makes the whole thing relatively simple! However, you can also make fine adjustments to the individual arm segments at any time. I hope you now have a good idea of what to expect from this model—but feel free to reach out via the comments if anything is unclear! The full Assembly guide can be found as a PDF in the „Assembly Guide“ section! In conclusion, I would aslo like to say a few things about printing: This project includes some very small parts—such as the printed dowel pins, which are only 2mm wide, used to assemble the excavator arm. It is therefore crucial that your print bed is very clean before printing this model! I used standard PLA for these profiles, but I am confident that most materials would perform well here, depending on your intended use for the model. For home use, PLA is perfectly adequate. If you plan to use the excavator outdoors, you might want to use a material like ASA. However, keep in mind that you may need to scale up the parts to compensate for shrinkage. As I mentioned earlier—and in the assembly instructions— material choice is most critical for the turntable component. It is not necessarily about the base material itself; PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, pure nylon, and many others would all work well. However, you should absolutely avoid printing this part using a material with a matte or rough surface finish. So, no matte PLA, no CF/GF (carbon or glass fiber), no glow-in-the-dark, and no sparkle filaments. Basically, nothing containing particles or fibers, and nothing with a matte finish. Please make sure to heed this advice! Otherwise, the servo driving the turntable will immediately let you know that it really doesn't appreciate the increased friction! Aside from that, I’d say this is a relatively easy model to print. Yes, it’s a multi-color print involving quite a few color changes, but even on a single-nozzle machine, the print time doesn't increase excessively, because it is already an extensive print anyway. When printing the lower section of the excavator tower or the decor elelents using a single-nozzle printer, you should either choose a color combination where the contrast in brightness isn't too extreme—unlike yellow and black—or increase purge volumes accordingly to prevent color bleed. Here is an example comparison image showing what can happen if insufficient material is purged during a color change, or when two materials with high contrast are used together. Feel free to let me know if you’d like to see a "no-AMS" profile. However, I do think the model loses a lot of its appeal without the multi-color aspect. The two main parts of the remote control—the housing and the faceplate—require a fair amount of support material. That said, almost all the less-than-perfect areas will be completely hidden once the model is assembled. I’m also considering offering a profile that uses a support interface; please let me know if there’s any interest in that. I really enjoy using those materials myself, though I realize it’s still somewhat of a niche practice. Be prepared to invest a fair amount of time if you want to slice this model yourself (starting from the provided STEP file). The model contains various "print-in-place" objects that first need to be isolated using the "Split to Parts" function, and so on. Therefore, if you wish to make any modifications, I recommend using my 3MF files as a starting point.This project includes some very small parts—such as the printed dowel pins, which are only 2mm wide, used to assemble the excavator arm. It is therefore crucial that your print bed is very clean before printing this model! I hope you like the project and have fun building and playing with it. Feel free to let me know if you’d like to see more Cyberbrick projects. However, my main focus—printer accessories—will remain, so don't worry :) Kind regards, Simon, Made In Meidling I

The on-device UI is modeled after my other project, FlightScnr : dark radar aesthetic, animated sweep, map tiles, and gesture navigation. A built-in web portal configures everything from your phone or laptop on the same network. What it does FlightScnr Pi shows live aircraft around your pre set location on a circular radar, with rich flight details when you tap a plane. It combines FlightRadar24 (FR24) , live positions from adsb.fi (free cloud feed — no local ADS-B dongle), Tomorrow.io weather , and optional AirLabs schedule data. Settings, API keys, tracking, and updates are managed through a local web portal. No SSH required for day-to-day use. Round touch display The UI is designed for a 4in round LCD with touch (default layout: 720x720 ). Screen How to open What you see Radar Boot / home Live aircraft, map background, sweep line, compass rose, range label, altitude tags Flight detail Tap aircraft on radar Airline logo, route, type, altitude, speed, heading; swipe or footer to cycle aircraft Tracked flight Web portal → Track, or swipe right on radar Route header, progress bar with aircraft icon, LIVE/ETA, vertical speed ticker; pin to keep screen open Clock and current weather Swipe down from radar Time, date, current weather and conditions Weather Forecast Swipe right from clock Multi-day forecast (Tomorrow.io) Clock settings Swipe left from clock Clock format and related options on-device About / details Swipe up from radar Version, network, API status, portal URL Settings Swipe left from radar Brightness, timeouts, color theme, display options (multi-page) Gestures and controls Tap aircraft → flight detail Tap range label (top) → cycle zoom presets (2–30 mi / km / nm) Two-finger pinch → zoom radar range in and out Swipe between screens (see table above) Footer buttons on detail, tracked, and settings screens (PREV / NEXT / RADAR / PIN) Auto-return to clock when no aircraft are visible (optional, portal setting) Off-hours schedule can dim the panel, turn it off, or force the clock screen at night Radar features Animated radar sweep with configurable accent color themes (Red, Yellow, Orange, Green, White) Optional compass rose and sweep line (toggle in portal) Map tile background (CARTO dark or OpenStreetMap) with cached tiles in /var/lib/flightscnr/maps/ Aircraft-type icons (jet, turboprop, helicopter, military, etc.) with altitude/speed tags Minimum altitude floor to hide low aircraft (e.g. pattern traffic) Alert mode : highlight military aircraft, emergency squawks (7700/7600/7500), or a custom watch list; optionally hide non-alerted traffic Distance units: km , statute miles , or nautical miles Tracked flight Pick any callsign in the web portal. The display shows origin → destination, aircraft type, a progress bar with a moving plane icon, and live stats (time remaining, distance, vertical speed). Flights not yet airborne can use AirLabs schedule data when configured. Web portal Open from any device on your LAN: http:// .local (default port 80 ; change with WEB_PORT in /etc/flightscnr.env) Section Purpose Radar Set radar center (lat/lon), range, distance units, min altitude, color theme, compass, sweep Display & screens Brightness, flight-detail and clock timeouts, auto-return to clock when empty Off-hours Night schedule - dim, turn off display, or show clock Weather °C / °F for clock and forecast Alerts Military, emergency squawk, watch list, hide non-alerted aircraft Tracking Track a callsign; route search (origin + destination) for live flights API keys FR24, Tomorrow.io, AirLabs - save or save & restart Updates Check GitHub for new releases; Update Now runs git pull and re-syncs (git checkout required) System Reboot or Shutdown the Pi remotely Portal preferences are stored on the Pi in /var/lib/flightscnr/ and apply without wiping on update. Data sources and modes Source Required? Provides FR24 API Yes (full app) Routes, airlines, flight details, tracked flights, enriched radar adsb.fi Optional (on by default) Free live positions over the internet — merges with FR24 or fills the radar when FR24 is off (ADSB_ENABLED=True). Not a USB ADS-B receiver. Tomorrow.io Yes (weather) Clock temperature and multi-day forecast AirLabs Optional Scheduled departure info when a tracked flight is not yet airborne API responses are cached (e.g. FR24 feed ~90s, flight details ~30 min, weather ~1 hr) to reduce quota use during 24/7 operation. Offline databases (airports.json, airlines.json, icao_types.json) download on first run. GitHub Link: https://github.com/yashmulgaonkar/FlightScnr_Pi

description: SIMPLE . FLYING . FUN Hummel RC is a simple and fun two-channel RC airplane designed for relaxed flights on a small field. Its modular construction is lightweight, durable and quick to print, with low material use and smooth, stable flight behavior. The adjustable wing position makes CG and pitch tuning easy. Hummel RC continues the ideas of WingStar , COMET , Wespe , SkyStar and DragonFly in a compact and practical RC model made to fly often . 1 - Model Data Wingspan: 405 mm Length: 365 mm Wing chord: 60 mm Model mass (with RC receiver, battery and motors): 43 g. 2 - Equipment RC transmitter and receiver: 2 Channel 2.4G FX803 J3 ( Aliexpress link here ) Battery: 3.7v, 220 mAh, Molex 51005 connector ( Aliexpress link here ) Motors and Props: 2x716 Coreless motors with 2 props diam 46 mm ( Aliexpress link here ) 3 - Materials, Settings, Printing Model design created and tested using Bambu PLA Basi c. Use this material for best results. Do NOT use PLA Matte, especially for the wing parts. Printed parts may deform after removal from the Plate due to internal material strains after cooling. Use recommended print settings. Note: The print profile for A1 mini use slightly higher material flow coefficient (1.03 instead of 0.98). For reliable printing: Clean the printing Plate before printing. After printing, remove the Plate and let it cool for 3-4 minutes Do not remove parts while the Plate is hot. 4 - Model Assembly The model consists of 20 parts, as shown in the figure. 1 – Nose, 2 – PCB Mount, 3 – A-Beam (3pcs), 4 – B-Beam, 5 – Strut (2pcs), 6 – Sting, 7 – Tail, 8 – Fin, 9 – Central Bracket, 10 – Dual-pin, 11 – Right Wing, 12 – Left Wing , 13 – Right Big Rib, 14 – Left Big Rib, 15 – Small Rib (2pcs), 16 – Gear mount, 17 – Gear Strut (2pcs), 18 – Wheel (2pcs), 19 – Pin (2pcs), 20 – BHCS Screw M2 x 4 mm (4 pcs). Note : RC Receiver, Engines, props are not shown. The following assembly steps are shown without the electronic components installed. It is recommended to review them before installing the motors and electronics. Use cyanoacrylate glue where specifically indicated. Assemble the tail unit and fuselage as shown. Assemble the wing as shown in the figure. Use Dual-pin to fix wings. After installing and fixing the wing surfaces, install Big Ribs (13, 14) on both sides. Finally, install the Ribs (15) on both sides. Wing assembly completed. To install the wing on the fuselage, pull the fuselage beam through predefined guide points on the wing Central Bracket, as shown in the picture. A slight pushing force may be gently applied if needed. Assemble landing gear unit as shown on Figure. Install landing gear on Fuselage. To fix finally the wing and landing gear position the M2x4 screws to be installed. Do not fix wing and gear assembly finally on this step! 4.1 - Electronic Components Installation Install RC transmitter PCB on bracket (2). Finally, connect the motors to the receiver board as shown in the illustration. Before final assembly, make sure the motors rotate in opposite directions. For easier assembly and adjustment, the wires should be approximately 130 mm long. The wires are preferable to route through the rib. To install the motor in the rib, gently press it into place and slide it slightly forward until there is no gap. To prevent the motor from rotating during operation, secure it with a small piece of adhesive tape, as shown in the illustration. Install the ribs with the motors onto the wing as shown in the illustration. The motors must be positioned on the outer side of each rib. Install the wing onto the lower beam, approximately at the middle of the span. Then route the motor wires behind the lower beam and around the upper beam in a figure-eight pattern, as shown in the illustration. This routing keeps the wires secure while still allowing the wing position to be adjusted. Only after routing the wires, install the landing gear, followed by the receiver bracket (2). Install the nose part (1) and secure it with screw (20). Install the battery and hold it in place with a suitable rubber band, as shown on picture. The model assembly is now complete. 4.2 - Balancing Perform the pre-flight balancing check with the battery installed. Place the model on a Balancing Stand ( model link here ) using the designated balance points on the wing. The model should remain level or tip slightly nose-down. Fix finally the screws (20) of wing assembly and gear bracket. 5 - Model Flight Launch the model outdoors in calm weather or slight breeze conditions. Recommended wind speed: up to 5 km/h (≈1.4 m/s, ≈2.7 knots) . Always launch the model directly into the wind . Model initially pre-balanced during assembly. Launch the model applying full throttle with a gentle horizontal push. If the model dives strongly, then: Move the wing slightly forward, OR bend the elevator slightly upward. If the model pitches up or stalls, first try reducing the flight speed. If flight speed reduction does not help, then: Move the wing slightly backward, OR bend the elevator slightly downward. Happy Flights and Smooth Landings!

Need a perfectly fitting plug for a tube, pipe, or custom hole? This fully parametric generator lets you create custom snap-fit end caps in seconds. Perfect for DIY projects, furniture, and custom enclosures. ⚙️ Customizable Parameters You can adjust the following settings to get a perfect fit for your specific use case: Cap Options (The top cover): cap_rad : The outer radius of the cap. cap_hight : The height/thickness of the cap itself. cap_fillet : Rounds the top edges of the cap for a smooth finish. Tube Options (The inserted part): tube_rad : The outer radius of the inserted tube section (match this to your hole). tube_hight : How deep the plug goes into the hole. tube_thickness : The wall thickness of the plug's stem. tube_fillet : Chamfers/rounds the bottom edge to make insertion easier. Snap-Fit & Flexibility Options: clip_size : The length of the retaining clips to lock the plug in place. (set do 0.001 for no clip) clip_angle : The angle of the clips (adjusts how easily it pushes in vs. pulls out). slit_width : The width of the relief slits. Wider slits make the plug more flexible for easier insertion. 💡 Printing Recommendations Material: PETG, ABS, or ASA are recommended for better flexibility and durability of the snap-fit clips. PLA works well for light-duty applications. Infill: 15-20% is usually sufficient. Supports: Not required if oriented flat on the cap.

model_name: Capsule Radar — Marine · Live AIS Ship Radar
description: A glowing round desk radar on a tilt stand that plots real ships around you from a live AIS feed — magnetic snap-on back, built-in alert speaker, flashed from your browser in a minute. No AMS; assembles with 6 magnets + 3 tiny screws. 🚢 Capsule Radar — Marine A polished desk gadget that turns the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75 (round 466×466 AMOLED, capacitive touch) into a live AIS ship radar . It pulls nearby vessels over WiFi and plots them on a glowing radar scope centred on your home, harbour, or a spot by a navigable river — useful by the coast and inland. Marine sibling of Capsule Radar (the aircraft version). Pick the Standard version (no case) or the -G (GPS, also fits). Avoid the "-B" — it comes with a protective case that won't fit; you'd have to remove it. (The separate "1.75C" is a different board — not this one.) ✨ Features Live vessel traffic on an animated radar scope with a rotating sweep + coastline map. Ship glyphs rotated by course (COG) , fading trails; anchored/moored vessels as quiet dots. Tap a vessel → name, distance, speed (SOG), course, heading, nav status, destination. Swipe between Radar / List / Stats; on-screen range button (2 / 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 nm); themes. Adjustable tilt stand to angle the scope just right. Magnetic snap-on back — fast, tool-light assembly. Built-in speaker for zone / proximity alert pings (e.g. a vessel entering the harbour). 🖨️ Printing — no AMS / no multi-material needed Each part prints in a single colour , so any printer works (I used a black case + orange stand). Parts: front case/bezel , magnetic back cover (+ speaker holder) , tilt stand . Material: PLA or PETG · Layer height: 0.2 mm · Walls: 3 · Infill: 15% Supports: minimal — only on the bezel ring that holds the screen . Total print time: ~2 hours . 🧰 What you need Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.75 board — buy it without the plastic case (this enclosure replaces it). USB-C data cable (power + flashing); optional 3.7 V LiPo (MX1.25) for cordless use. 6× ⌀6 × 2 mm neodymium disc magnets (press-fit — 3 in the case, 3 in the back cover). 3× M2 × 6 mm screws to fasten the screen/board to the bezel ring. The Waveshare speaker (MX1.25) for alert sounds (optional). The tilt pivot uses printed pins — no hardware there. A free aisstream.io API key (non-commercial) for the live feed. 🔩 Assembly (easy — no tools) Press-fit the 6 magnets into the case and back cover. Screw the screen to the bezel ring with the 3× M2×6 screws. Plug the speaker into the SPK connector and tuck it into the back. Snap the magnetic back on. Clip the case into the tilt stand with the printed pins ; angle to taste. Flash & set up (next). ⚡ Flash & set up — no toolchain Get a free AIS API key at aisstream.io → sign up → Create API Key (free, non-commercial, no credit card). description: Why? I'm a huge fan of calisthenics. Over 5 years ago I decided I needed a regimen that could travel with me anywhere, with minimal equipment. Then I would never have an excuse to miss. Pull-ups while traveling can be a challenge. Sometimes there's a playground nearby, sometimes the hotel actually has a pull-up bar. And sometimes there's nothing (work takes me to remote areas). The 70 mm version can fit everything on a single 256x256 plate, 90 mm will have to be done in pieces. If you're using this for hotel door frames, you never know what size they may have … choose wisely (or print both). Arm: “Small boy” arm is 32 mm deep and 40 mm wide. "Big boy” arm is 32 mm deep and 60 mm wide. Handle: 28 mm diameter (easier to grip but can be more painful). 32 mm diameter (harder to grip but can be less painful). Both are common options with gymnastics rings. SAFETY You are responsible for ensuring your printer, materials, slicer settings, door frame, paracord and use of the provided files and instructions are sufficient to ensure your safety. Testing I weigh 215 lbs. and am wearing a 40 lbs. weighted vest in the torture test you see. Note that I used an earlier and weaker prototype of the “small boy” version . The weakest link is the handle, be sure to properly thread your paracord. I'm confident that if you use the correct filament and settings, and don't put 300+ lbs. on one side, you should be okay. ASSEMBLY & USE Arrange the arms so that the “hands” face each other, like a claw. Slide the pin through the large center hole. You can thread it so that the handle is perpendicular to the door frame or at a 45 degree angle (see examples in the photos). Open the arms and carefully place over the door frame (if you're concerned about the wall or casing finish, put some electrical tape on the edges that make contact). Grab the handles and slowly lower yourself, shifting your weight to the system (note: the paracord and knot will work out some slack, and you'll shift downward a little).

Most 3D-printed phone docks with "speakers" sound pretty bad. They usually just punch a straight, hollow cone into a block of plastic, which traps the low frequencies and makes your phone sound like it’s playing out of a tin can. I wanted a dock that actually worked, and I wanted it to look like a piece of high-end vintage audio gear on my desk. The Monolith hides a mathematically calculated, 100mm exponential horn inside a solid, minimalist block. Instead of just bouncing sound forward, the internal sweep acts as a true acoustic transformer—just like an old-school gramophone. It physically amplifies the volume and actually brings back the warmth and bass of your phone's speaker without using any electricity. Because phone cases make finding a good dock impossible, I built this to be fully parametric in MakerLab. There's pre-sets for different phones with and without phone cases and I also allow for custom measurements. Just hit the Customize button . Features Fits Your Exact Phone Setup: No more wobbly phones or slots that are too tight. Pick your phone model from the dropdown, then choose your case type (Bare Phone, Slim Case, or Heavy Duty Armor). The customizer calculates the exact tolerances so your phone slides in perfectly. Audiophile vs. Charging Mode: By default, the acoustic chamber is sealed airtight for maximum volume. But if you’d rather use this as an overnight charging dock, just check the "Enable Charging Channel" box. It routes a massive 16mm internal tunnel that easily swallows thick, braided USB-C cables. Supported Device Presets The Monolith's customizer includes precise base dimensions (Width x Thickness) for the following devices. You can select your exact phone model and then pair it with your case type for a perfect fit. Apple iPhone 17 Series iPhone 17 Pro Max: 77.6 mm x 8.3 mm iPhone 17 Pro: 71.5 mm x 8.3 mm iPhone 17: 71.5 mm x 8.0 mm iPhone Air: 74.7 mm x 5.6 mm Apple iPhone 16 Series iPhone 16 Pro Max: 77.6 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 16 Pro: 71.5 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 16: 71.6 mm x 7.8 mm Apple iPhone 15 Series iPhone 15 Pro Max: 76.7 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 15 Pro: 70.6 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 15: 71.6 mm x 7.8 mm Google Pixel Series (Note: All Pixel presets automatically generate an additional 2.5mm of pocket depth to allow the camera visor to sit flush without snagging). Pixel 10 Pro XL: 76.6 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 10: 72.2 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9 Pro XL: 76.6 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9 Pro: 72.0 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9: 72.0 mm x 8.5 mm Samsung Galaxy Series Galaxy S26 Ultra: 79.0 mm x 8.6 mm Custom Devices Don't see your phone? Select the Custom option in the dropdown and manually enter your phone's width and thickness! Case Allowances Once you select your phone model, choose your case style. The generator automatically adds the necessary tolerances to your phone's base dimensions: Bare Phone: Adds +0.5 mm clearance for a snug, scratch-free fit. Slim Case: Adds +5.0 mm clearance for standard silicone and leather cases. Heavy Duty Armor: Adds +12.0 mm clearance for rugged, multi-layer cases. Print Instructions (Read Before Slicing!) Supports: OFF. Seriously, do not use supports. If you do, the slicer will fill the internal acoustic chamber with grid plastic, and you will never get it out. The printer will bridge the internal gaps on its own. Infill: 10% Rectilinear is fine. Walls: 2 walls min but 3 walls is default (better acoustics). Denser plastic means less sound bleeds through the sides, forcing all the audio energy out the front bell. Drop a make if you print one, and let me know how it sounds!

I really like the design of BeamCase and I wanted a smaller version of it. So what I have created is basically that. I have based some of the design on the BeamCase (designed from scratch) - mainly the truss on the mobo tray. The case is not modular, there is only one 5.5L version - and I won't be making any other versions of it. Specs: 5.5L volume (not accounting for panels) Max 47mm cooler height Max 2 slot 200mm GPU Flex ATX PSU 90mm fans at the top - brackets are made for Noctua NF-A9x14 which are 14.5mm thick Filament: Frame - I've used Bambu Labs PETG-HF, but according to the internet It would be best if you used ABS or ASA for the internal parts, although you will need to take the shrinkage into the account Panels - Does not really matter, PLA is fine. I used Polymer Panchroma PLA Matte Lime Green Note on seams: If you want to use raw STLs, make sure the seams for the brackets that go into the T-Slots are NOT anywhere near the T-Slots. I have manually painted seams in the included profile to avoid that. Note on panels: Panels are in a separate print profile and have an internal infill-based pattern - which means you can control it in the slicer. I am partial to triangles but you can set it up however you want :) You will get better results using thicker nozzles, I've used 0.6mm - 0.4mm works ok too but the panels are a bit less rigid. Parts needed: 200mm double reverse PCI-E riser - Specifically this one (4.0) from Aliexpress Bracket is made to fit only this riser but I've included step file so you can modify it to fit yours 16mm push button for power button - you can buy it pre-made, I soldered my own, cable length should be ~20cm Hardware needed: 1010 T-Slot Makerbeam 200mm extrusion profiles T-Slot M3 Nuts from Makerbeam Countersunk M3 screws, just buy a whole bag of each, you can use them in different projects :) 6mm 8mm 12mm 16mm PSU - #6-32 x 3/8" UNC screws - I bought these M3 nuts Note: I take no responsibility for you breaking your potentially expensive PC parts. You are building this case at your own risk, so double-check clearances, whether you are using the correct length of screws, support heavy components, and proceed carefully. I only tested it with my own components and I cannot guarantee it will fit your exact configuration. Components I have used for my build: Mobo - Asrock B550M-ITX/ac Cooler - Thermalright AXP90-X47 Full Copper CPU Fan - NF-A12x15 with this bracket that I've slightly modified PSU - Enhance ENP-7660L-OVT GPU - Powercolor Radeon 9060XT Reaper Assembly Instructions: Here are all the 3D printed parts that you will need: (apart from the gpu bracket locker which I realised I forgot to print, it's present in subsequent pics) Tools that you will need: M3 driver - hex key is fine too but you will need more elbow grease Electric screwdriver with M3 bit (H2) - technically not necessary, but it will make it much easier Prepping the parts Insert hex nuts in correct places and press them in. 2 on the front of the mobo tray 4 on the back of the mobo tray 2 in the back of the case (power button) 2 in the gpu bracket locker 2 in the back of the pcie riser You should prepare the beams (inserting Makerbeam T-Slot nuts on the sides) before you start putting the case together. It will be really annoying to do afterwards - so my suggestion is to triple check everything and try to imagine how it will go together (feel free to scroll down to use the pics to help your imagination). The holes for panels are lined up exactly with the T-Slot nuts - on end positions. Note: The parts (brackets) that you insert into the beams have the T-Slot shaped in a way where you will be essentially “shaving” off a sliver of plastic when inserting them. That's by design, I found it gives the best fit. So if they do not “go in” all the way, take it out, flip them out, clear out the plastic shavings and try again. Top beams Insert fan brackets and push them towards the center Insert end brackets, holes should be facing outwards Insert T-Slot nuts in places where you will be mounting the panels - so, 2 on the top, 2 on each sides Push the fans into the brackets Bottom beams Insert end bracket - I am using a custom one made for Enhance ENP-7660L-OVT PSU (included in the files), so if you will be using the generic one, it will look slightly different. Frame Screw the back of the case to the mobo tray using 16mm screws Note: You will be screwing into the plastic and essentially threading it, so electric screwdriver with M3 bit is recommended. Don't screw them in fully with the electric screwdriver though or you'll risk stripping the threads. Use a normal M3 driver for that. Stop when you encounter too much resistance. Motherboard I would suggest prepping the motherboard first (cpu, cooler, ram, storage). I've also inserted the pcie riser and power cables cause I found it annoying to do it after the case is put together. Note: The case itself is held together by 4 screws at this point, so I would suggest laying it on the corner of a desk/table so that you do not put unnecessary stress on the plastic parts at this point. Insert the IO shield for the motherboard Put the motherboard on the motherboard posts Put 4 x 16mm screws through the spacers that you have printed Screw the motherboard into the tray PCI-E Riser Bracket Install the PCIE riser bracket with 12mm screws to the back of the mobo tray PSU You can put your PSU in and secure it to the back of the case with #6-32 x 3/8" screws This will allow to put the case vertically and the weight of the mobo tray will rest on the PSU for now Make sure your pcie riser was inserted and routed by this point and it goes above the PSU Bottom Beams You can now slide the bottom beams with brace installed and screw them in from the back of the case with 16mm screws If you are using Enhance ENP-7660L-OVT PSU then you can screw it to the custom brace using #6-32 x 3/8" screws Power button Unscrew the nut from your 16mm power button, put it through the power button plate, screw the nut in Put the cable through the back of the case and screw the plate into the back of the case with 6mm screws GPU Connect the GPU to the riser Put the GPU into the case Line up the holes from the pcie riser to the ones on the pcie riser bracket Screw the pcie riser into the pcie riser bracket using 8mm screws - leave it a bit loose for now, as in don't screw it in fully - this will make it easier to line up everything properly Insert the gpu bracket that "plugs" the hole on the back of the case - you might need to push the gpu upwards a little bit Screw in 12mm screws from the top to secure the gpu - you might need to push the gpu towards the mobo tray to wiggle them in - hold your finger underneath the nuts, they might pop out Front Line it up to the mobo tray Install the front of the frame to the mobo tray using 16mm screws It might help if you temporarily screw in the front to the bottom beams to line it up better. Put the top beams on and route fan cables accordingly Secure all the braces with 12mm (not 16mm!!) screws from the outside. Done, you've built the frame :) Panels Now the only thing remaining is to put on the panels. Mount side, top and bottom panels with 6mm screws Mount the front panel with 16mm screws

Il suffit d'y glisser les bouteilles congelées : l'air propulsé par les pales se refroidit instantanément au contact de la glace. Fixation modulable : Le créateur a intégré des fentes sur le modèle. Si l'accroche d'origine ne suffit pas ou si vous voulez bloquer le système, vous pouvez utiliser des serre-câbles ( zip ties ) pour le fixer solidement à la grille. Astuce pratique : N'oubliez pas de placer une petite serviette ou un récipient sous le ventilateur pour récupérer l'eau de condensation qui va perler le long des bouteilles.

Here's my take on a guitar → hurdy gurdy style conversion kit. This is a v1.0 release, so I would love to hear your feedback on improvements. You will need to source o-rings and dark rosin to use this as intended. I highly suggest checking out assembly instructions to make things clear on how to properly mount it without damaging anything on your guitar. How it works: It' fastened to the bottom and top string of your guitar and plays on the four middle strings using two o-rings coated with rosin. This creates friction which then vibrate the strings when cranking the wheel. Tips: Using rosin on the o-rings is required, it won't work well without it. Check out part list for more details. It's easier to tune the strings after you've installed the o-rings and before you assemble the Gurdy Wheel. DADA tuning works great, as well as GDAE. Extras: If your guitar has a pick guard, you can print out the + 2mm height foot to offset the height difference. If you need more tension on the o-rings you can use two +2 mm feet instead of the default ones. To apply rosin to the o-rings, use sandpaper or a knife to break up the rosin and slide the o-rings gently across the surface to coat them. Print out TPU feet if you are having issues with movement of the whole assembly when cranking. Also protects your guitar body. O-rings can possibly be printed and are provided with the print profile, but would need to be as soft as possible, as industry o-rings tend to be around 60-70A on the shore hardness scale. I've tried with 95A and that did not work. You can print the bearings and screw if you don't have the hardware available, but I highly recommend steel bearings and bolt for less play between the parts. Larger handle is provided in the print profile if you feel the small one does not suit you. Disclaimer: May or may not work on your exact guitar model. I've tested it on three different guitars and they all worked, but with different neck widths it's hard to say how it will perform on your particular model. I'm in no way responsible for any damage that may occur to your guitar during installation.

description: A compact handle with an integrated spring-loaded auto-latch. Simply pull the release pin to open, and the latch automatically engages again when closing. See GIF in the gallery. The design is suitable for a wide range of doors, gates, hatches, enclosures, or other DIY projects where a simple automatic latching mechanism is desired. Features: Spring-loaded automatic latching Robust construction One-handed operation Easy to assemble No AMS required, prints without supports With a drilling template for easy alignment Tip: Start by printing just the drilling template if you want to get a feel for the size Assembly: Part overview: Press the pin into the sliding latch: If it is not fitting perfect you could scale the pin in bambu studio. Attach the sliding latch into the handle: Add the cover plate. The cover is designed to fit loosely on the handle. Stability is achieved later using the two screws. Attach the cover plate for the latch keeper. Mounting it on the door/gate etc: Use the drilling template to mark the positions of the 4 screws with a pencil. Now pre-drill these holes with a suitable drill bit. Use 4 countersunk screws, size 4x45 mm, or ideally 4x50 mm. 3.5x45 mm / 3.5x50 mm should also work. Adjustable for Offset Installations The design works with both flush and offset installations. If the two mounting surfaces are not aligned, simply scale the Latch Keeper in the slicer along its height by the same amount as the offset. This keeps the latch perfectly aligned and ensures reliable operation. Example: If the frame extends 10 mm further than the door or gate, scale the Latch Keeper 10 mm shorter in height. This keeps the latch aligned. Print settings: All parts can be printed without supports Add extra walls/infill for the parts: Both cover plates and the sliding latch Filament: The spring was successfully tested with PLA Basic and PETG. If you want to use the model outdoors, I recommend PETG, ABS, or, ideally, ASA.

================================ 📋 Recommended Print Settings (For Best Results) Filament: PLA. Different materials have different shrink rates, so using other filaments might cause fitting issues or dimensional errors during assembly. Slicer: Bambu Studio. I recommend using my default profile — I’ve tuned it specifically for this model. Ambient Temperature: If you’re using an open-frame printer like the A1 or A1 Mini, keep your room above 20°C (68°F) to prevent warping. Print Bed Preparation: Wash with soap and water, then dry thoroughly to ensure good adhesion. For small parts, apply a glue stick for better bed adhesion. 🔧 Assembly Diagram Notes Blue Lines: Require super glue for assembly. I use Gorilla Super Glue. Yellow Lines: These are moving parts. Do not apply glue here. Before installing the tank’s side skirts, please first fit the front road wheels and rear road wheels. The recommended assembly order is: Install the front idler wheels and rear drive sprockets (front and rear wheels) Attach the side skirts Then install the remaining road wheels in the middle

description: Behold! After months of design and testing in my free time, I am finally at a point where I can confidently post these files to the public. This design features a conversion kit for the P365 platform from Sig. This is a “drop-in” conversion kit that features pic rails and a charging handle for easier functionality. The main chassis of this model was designed as one whole piece and then split in half in the slicer so that it can be 3D printed on the split line and then mated together with bolts/screws. This was my design intent as it reduced any chances of failure due to layer adhesion and it seemed to be the strongest print orientation for this project. I have meticulously designed the chassis to clamp onto the front rails on the P365 frame and have also incorporated rear locking plates to keep the beavertail on the frame locked into place. This proved to be difficult because there are two different types of beaver tails that come with the P365 platform so I had to make a version for each one. I then designed a “charging handle” that rests on the slide over the rear sight so you can manipulate the firearm while it’s in the chassis. Last but not least, there is an angled magazine holder included in this design that is specifically meant to clip onto the front pic rail of this chassis. This attachment allows you to store an extra magazine on your kit, and it also serves as a crucial clamping point for the chassis/handgun connection. This specific attachment is not required for the functionality of the conversion kit but you must have something mounted to the front pic rail in order to fully lock the chassis (This will be explained further in the assembly guide). I am releasing three version of this conversion kit; the normal closed version (original), the MLOK version (closed version with added MLOK mounts), and the open version (front opened up). You are able to choose whichever one you like best and you can even mix and match the halves since they are symmetrical. Note: THESE FILES ARE INTENDED ONLY AS ACCESSORY COMPONENTS FOR INSTALLATION ON A LAWFULLY OWNED, COMMERCIALLY MANUFACTURED FIREARM. THEY DO NOT INCLUDE FILES FOR ANY COMPONENT THAT IS LEGALLY CLASSIFIED AS A FIREARM UNDER APPLICABLE LAW. YOU ASSUME ALL RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH THE MANUFACTURE, ASSEMBLY, AND USE OF ANY PRINTED OR FABRICATED COMPONENTS. NONE OF THE INCLUDED MODELS CAN BE ASSEMBLED TO MAKE A FIREARM ON THEIR OWN. YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR COMPLYING WITH ALL OF YOUR LOCAL/FEDERAL LAWS WHEN MAKING THIS. NEVER ASSEMBLE THIS KIT WITH A LOADED FIREARM. Final Thoughts: This was originally a personal project that I wanted to make mainly to improve my CAD skills, but also to see if it was even possible to do with a real firearm. The looks or aesthetics of this design was an afterthought as the main focus was strength and function. I designed and redesigned multiple components of this project over the course of many months and I am very happy with the way it turned out. It’s not 100% “drop-in” as some screws have to be tightened after installing the handgun but it is as close as I could get it without introducing any crazy hardware pieces. Feedback is appreciated, enjoy! Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 4-part mould (3 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with a smooth design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould three times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 6.5cm diameter and 7cm height, or a capacity of around 150ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 75ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier.

Dieses rechteckige Lüftungsgitter ist voll anpassbar, d.h. die meisten Parameter können eingestellt werden. Optional kann auch ein sehr feines passendes Insektenschutzgitter ergänzt werden, das hinten in das Lüftungsgitter gesteckt wird. Mögliche Einstellungen für das Lüftungsgitter Breite, Höhe, Tiefe und Dicke des Rahmens, der in die Öffnung (Wand, Schrank) eingesteckt wird. Breite der vorderen Blende - wie viel soll über die Wand nach außen ragen und wie viel soll nach innen überlappen Lamellen: Länge, Winkel, Dicke. Und ein Faktor, der bestimmt, ob sie genau die Sicht verdecken (Faktor=1) oder größere Lücken lassen (Faktor > 1) oder dichter sind (Faktor < 1) Querstreben: Die Querstreben dienen der Stabilisierung und lassen das Gitter auch “professioneller” aussehen. Einstellbar sind Anzahl, Dicke und Tiefe. Außerdem kann man wählen, ob sie 5 mm nach hinten versetzt werden sollen. Das sieht noch sauberer aus, erfordert aber das Drucken mit Stützstrukturen. Das von mir eingestellte Druckprofil hat bereits die entsprechenden Einstellungen. Hilfreiches Es gibt eine englische und eine deutsche Version der Einstellungs-Datei. Du brauchst ein rundes Lüftungsgitter? Das findest du hier . Insektenschutz Das Insektenschutzgitter ist optional und kann hinten in das Lüftungsgitter eingelegt werden, um selbst sehr kleine Insekten fernzuhalten. Ich habe es in ein separates Projekt ausgelagert, um es auch für andere Lüftungsgitter-Modelle verfügbar zu machen: Insektenschutz für Lüftungsgitter Die Maße müssen passend zum Lüftungsgitter eingestellt werden. Dabei muss die Wandstärke berücksichtigt werden: X: Breite - 2 * Wandstärke Y: Höhe - 2 * Wandstärke Z: nicht ändern, auf 1 mm lassen Beispiel: Maße des Teils, das in die Wandöffnung gesteckt wird: 100 x 200 mm. Wandstärke 3 mm Dann muss das Insektenschutzgitter die Größe 94 x 194 haben, denn X=100-2*3=94 und Y=200-2*3=194 Wie immer freue ich mich über Kommentare und Feedback, Verbesserungsvorschläge oder Wünsche. description: # ⚙️ Ultimate Parametric Gear Generator (Involute & Double/Step Gears) This is a highly precise, fully parametric **Spur Gear and Double/Step Gear Generator** designed specifically for 3D printing and mechanical engineering. Using the **MakerWorld Customizer**, you can create custom gears directly in your browser without any CAD knowledge! It uses true mathematical **involute tooth geometry**, ensuring smooth rotation, low friction, and maximum durability for your custom gearboxes, robotics, or RC projects. --- ### 🚀 Key Features * **True Involute Teeth:** Mathematically correct tooth profiles that roll smoothly without jamming. * **Double / Step Gear Option:** Easily stack two custom gears on a single shaft. Perfect for compound gear trains and high-reduction gearboxes! * **D-Cut / D-Shaft Support:** Toggle a flat side (D-cut) inside the bore to perfectly fit NEMA stepper motors or RC motors. * **Fully Parametric:** Adjust Module (size), Tooth Count, Gear Thickness, and Shaft Diameter with simple sliders. * **No External Libraries:** 100% standalone OpenSCAD script, perfectly compatible with the MakerWorld cloud compiler. --- ### 🔧 How to Customize Your Gear 1. Click on the **Open in Customizer** button on MakerWorld. 2. **Gear 1 (Base):** Set your desired tooth count, thickness, and Module (defines tooth size, standard is 2.0). 3. **Gear 2 (Step Gear):** Check `z2_aktiv` to add a secondary gear on top, or uncheck it for a standard single gear. 4. **Bore & Axis:** Set your shaft diameter. If you use a D-shaft motor, check `d_cut_aktiv` and define the flat width. 5. Click **Generate** and download your 3D-printable `.STL` file! --- ### 🖨️ Recommended Print Settings * **Material:** PETG, ABS, ASA, or Nylon for functional parts. PLA is fine for prototyping or low-load toys. * **Wall Loops:** 4 to 6 walls (perimeters) for maximum tooth strength. * **Infill:** 40% - 100% (Gyroid recommended). * **Top/Bottom Layers:** 5 layers. * **Cooling:** Keep it balanced to ensure great layer adhesion on the teeth.

Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 4-part mould (3 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with an angular design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould three times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 6.5cm diameter and 7cm height, or a capacity of around 150ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 75ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier.
