description: This model is the HO-scale version of the third in a series of “Thinline Scale Model” structure kits for Z-scale and N-scale model railroading. The Z-scale and N-scale kits are available here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/3025340-trackside-factory-tsm-03-for-z-n-scale#profileId-3399541 . The Trackside Factory (HO-scale edition) - This structure kit is for a factory that could be located off of a track siding. For my layout, the Z-scale version of this factory will be receiving lumber from a lumber mill down the line and producing wood-based products, such as furniture, for shipping out to market via the railroad. To see other kits in this series please visit my collection page: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/15297762-model-train-projects . I designed this model in SolidWorks inspired by an original design by a former member of our Z-scale modeling club - he did market a laser-cut wood kit for a short while (as fannocreek designs) but alas those kits are no longer available so he graciously gave me permission to craft my model as a likeness of his. Given my model is for 3d-printing, I've completely re-engineered the way that the kit is made and assembled, and I've made other design changes based on how some interior aspects of the factory would change some of the exterior appearance. And, after many failed attempts to recreate an exposed support structure under the trackside dock and front deck that would print reliably in one piece, I chose to enclose the underside of both dock and deck. Important Note: Before proceeding to print and build this kit, please note the following requirements needed to produce good results. Also, please read through the entire description to understand all of the assembly steps required. For printing, a 0.4mm nozzle and a clean build plate is required - this model profile specifically uses a 0.20mm layer layer height given that its a scaled design from the Z-scale model which requires a 0.2mm nozzle and a 0.08mm layer height (0.08 x 220/87 = 0.20229 rounds to 0.20). This kit includes both two-color and three-color prints - an AMS is required . Supplied needed: fast setting (5-10 seconds) CA adhesive; and a selection of acrylic paints / brushes for painting the model (if desired). Tools needed: a good bed scraper tool for removing some of the parts from the build plate - I found the bed scraping blade supplied with the printers by Bambu Lab to work well for this purpose (most beneficial was its thin sharp blade for lifting very thin prints . The Print Profiles - Three profiles are available for this structure kit, the profiles generally differ by single ( P1S , A1 , H2S , etc.) and dual-nozzle ( H2D and H2C ) printers, and also an A1 Mini -specific profile. Please note that all of the profiles include a number of parameter changes from the standard print profiles that probably should not be tampered with if you want good results. One of the more important profile variances is that I've significantly slowed down the nozzle speed, travel speed and acceleration to help assure the best result printing the detail features of these models - I've specifically supplied separate profiles based on direct-drive nozzle count because changing the printer of a single-nozzle profile to a dual-nozzle printer (and vice versa) may cause the speed settings to be lost in the profile. I highly recommend that you use the appropriate single or dual-nozzle profile matching your printer capability. Note: I've included X2D with the A1 profile primarily because of the build plate size … if you choose to take advantage of the auxiliary nozzle, just be aware that this model relies on being able to print some very fine detail. Important note regarding the factory name: The original laser-cut wood kit included decals for naming the factory, a choice of either “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” or “ TELLER & SONS MFG ”, the latter one being the one I'm planning to use on my Z-scale layout. For the HO-scale profiles, I've included both naming options with the “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” as the default choice - if you prefer “ TELLER & SONS MFG ” on your model, find the build plate where the wall with the name appears and deselect the named wall you don't want and select the named wall that you do want. Make sure that only one of these walls are selected for printing … if both are selected, Bambu Studio should complain and you will need to deselect one to proceed; if none are selected, you will be missing a wall in the print so make that one is selected. If you have questions about any of this, please feel free to reach out to me. One final note … you can optionally remove the name from the wall by deleting the text element, or you can attempt to change the name to something you prefer but please note that you should take care to recenter, left to right, the text on the wall after you edit the name. Also note that the text tool when used on a textured surface such as these walls can be a bit finicky with sometimes distorting the placement of individual characters so you might have to mess around with it a bit to get it to behave. I've taken some care to make sure that the text fits nicely when positioned vertically across the siding boards. And finally, most of the text fonts available will not print well at these scales which is why I've focused on the two sans-serif fonts used in the profile. Choosing Filaments - In my profiles, I've chosen to use Bambu Lab PLA Matte filaments as I prefer the surface finish over PLA Basic . With the model based on four colors as set in the profiles, all of the major elements of the model could be left as printed but there are a small number of details that I recommend be painted to help finish the model (see below for painting recommendations). I've tried to minimize the number of color changes needed on each build plate in the profiles to keep purge waste as low as possible. === ASSEMBLY INSTRUCTIONS === These diagrams provides a general overview of the kit parts. === Painting and Window Glazing Recommendations === At a minimum, I would suggest adding some diluted color washes to give a more weathered look to the structure. Before assembling the kits in the photos, I choose to paint the lower masonry block surfaces of the two white bases to help bring out the detail. I first coated the masonry surfaces with a white acrylic gesso and after that dried thoroughly, I worked it over with a thinned coat of ‘tarnished’ black, the gesso helps to create a more receptive surface for the paint on the plastic. For those interested, here is an Amazon link to the Micro-Mark Acrylic paints I've used on my models: https://a.co/d/0fMC2PB2. There are a number of details in this kit that should be painted prior to assembly. This include the two chimneys, the utility cabinet, the shipping crates, and the firebox as seem in the following photo. The firebox is an integrated feature of the middle wall and it takes a bit of extra care in painting it without getting paint on the wall siding (blue) - note that I chose to paint the lid in gray with the rest of the box in red. For the crates, I only chose to dirty them up a bit to help differentiate them from the dock color. Note: If you choose to change the filament colors to either reduce the number of filaments or simply to picking more neutral colors with a plan of painting the model, you should consider painting individual parts prior to assembly although adding weathering detail is often done with the overall model built up. Using some paint color washes can help enhance the details while also making the building not appear as it was just build yesterday :-). If you want to add window glazing (simulated window glass), I would suggest that being done either before attaching the walls to the base, or at least right after attaching the walls to the base - going beyond those steps in the assembly process will make it difficult to adding glazing. You also need to consider that if you are painting the model, care must be taken to not get paint on your window glazing so the painting versus glazing order becomes important. I'm still messing around with different techniques for glazing 3d-printed models … either using a clear film/plastic material or something like this clear adhesive by Microscale Industries ( https://a.co/d/0gy3e33L ) that can also be used to form small windows on models (this stuff can be a bit tricky to get it to work right but I've successfully used similar, unfortunately discontinued by Micro-Mark , products in the past. === Starting with some sub-assemblies === There are a number of sub-assemblies to complete prior to starting the general assembly of the kit. It is recommended that before applying adhesive, you study all of the photos closely to see how parts are supposed to fit once assembled. Once each is completed, set it aside until needed in the general assembly. The fire escape Note the alignment of the underside notches of the ladder to the support features of the wall - make sure to get the ladder in the proper orientation with the shorter piece of the ladder above the top notch and the longer piece of the ladder below the bottom notch (and extending below the wall once attached. Also take care to center the latter, left to right, on the provided supports. Note the alignment of the escape platform with the two provided wall supports centered beween the platform leg structures. The winch support beams The winch supports are two small parts that look somewhat like mini-tripods. Note the alignment of the winch support relative to the top of the door and the notch in the wall. The awning platforms with supports Note that the support legs have bumps that fit into the underside slots of the awning bases. Also note that the leg of the support is positioned closest to the thinner edge of the awning base. Key to this sub-assembly is to make sure that the supports sit flush against the surface of the base with the leg standing straight up, left to right, from the base. The larger awning platform is for the trackside dock and the smaller one is for the front deck. The clerestory Note that the four walls fit well within the inside cavity of the main roof beam base. Once they are in position with all of the wall edges lined up and with the walls firmly seated down within the cavity, add the adhesive drops where the walls meet and with a couple more at the base on the longer walls down where they meet the base, and hold everything in position, making sure not to disrupt that the wall edges appear properly aligned with no obvious gaps. The upper beam can then be added with adhesive on the small flat surfaces of the beam to glue to the inside of the end walls when set into the alignment gaps. The right-side chimney Note that the chimney needs to be inserted from the underside of the roof section and oriented with the thicker side of the chimney wedge base positioned toward the large gap side of the roof. Once you have the chimney firmly seated flush to the underside of the roof, apply some adhesive to hold it in place. The chimney wedged base serves to orient the chimney vertical once the roof is installed on the model. Now you should have the following sub-assemblies ready for use when starting the general assembly of the factory. === Assembling the factory === The base Each of the interlocking tabs on the left-side base, the trackside dock and the front deck have corresponding receiving slots on the right-side base, and for the dock and deck, also on the left-side base. Gently press each tab into its corresponding slot and work each in until its fully inserted and flush … it helps to place the assembly on a solid surface and press things down from the top but be careful to not damage any of the other features on the bases when doing this … I've strengthened the underside of the bases in the areas around the slots to facilitate pressing down in those areas. While these four parts are designed to hold together without need for gluing, you may choose to add some CA adhesive to the mating joints underneath once the parts are mated up flush together. The right-side walls Note: The key to having nice corners between walls of this model are to focus on the close alignment of each wall edge relative to the adjacent wall edge when holding them together while the adhesive takes hold. There should be no significant gaps, top to bottom, along the mating edges. Before adding adhesive to glue in any of the walls, please do a test fit to make sure that the wall edges will align nicely when finally set in place. [This actually takes a bit more effort on this HO-scale version of the model than it does on the smaller scale versions as the mating surfaces are quite a bit larger.] Start with the middle wall … note the alignment notch position where the middle should lock into place. Make sure that the wall sits flush with the side of the stairway and other vertical features of the base. Next is the back wall … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and at points along the bottom edge … if all goes according to plan, once in place, the edge between the middle and back walls should line up very nicely. Continue with the front wall (with the name) … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and at points along the bottom edge. Next is installing the second floor insert … note the orientation of the second floor insert and how it aligns at the top of the stairway. Apply adhesive drops at the tops of the vertical features of the base and then place the second floor insert within the structure and flush down on those features. After the floor is in place, you may choose to add some more adhesive to help secure the front and back walls to the second floor. Finally, adding the right-side wall sub-assembly with the fire escape … take care not to damage the ladder when handling this wall section. Again, apply small adhesive drops to the exposed surfaces where the wall will sit. The left-side walls Starting with the back wall, apply small adhesive drops where shown and assure that the wall is flush with the base alignment edge and vertical features once in place. Next, add the front wall ... Finally, add the left-side wall using the vertical surface of the fireplace feature for adhesive and as a supporting surface for the wall. The awnings Each awning sub-assembly has three slots that are designed to align with the three support tabs on the left-side front and back walls. To install each awning sub-assembly, gently press the slots over the corresponding tabs … make sure to not damage the awning support legs while doing this … the tabs will fit rather snugly, so take it slow as you go. I generally start with one of the end slots followed by the opposite end slot, making sure that the middle slot is in its proper place as I start to press them together. I then work each tab into the slots a little bit each at a time, rotating between them until they are all fully inserted. Place a finger inside the wall behind each tab as support while pressing the awning base flush to the outside of the wall. No adhesive is needed at this point. Repeat with the awning against the back wall, and again work each tab just a bit at a time, rotating between them until they are all finally fully inserted. Make sure that the awning bases are flush with the walls before proceeding … it may take some persuasion but do be careful to not damage anything while working them on. Now is time to install the awning top surfaces. Examine the awning surface parts closely … note that one of the long edges of each will have a complete shingle row and the other a partial one, the partial row should end up mounted close to the wall so that the complete row of shingles is exposed along the outer edge of the awning. Apply adhesive drops along the edges close to the wall and the outside edge of the awning. (If, as you move the awning surface pieces into place, a bit of adhesive gets pushed up into the crack where the awning base is pressed against the wall, that would not be a bad thing :o). Now it is time to add some adhesive to keep the awning legs in the proper place … for this, you will need either a toothpick or another way to gab a small drop of adhesive behind each of the legs where they will sit up against the leg alignment features of the dock and deck. Each leg should be positioned just in front of and centered on each alignment bump … the legs are a bit flexible and move easily at this point so dab on a small drop of adhesive just behind the lower back portion of the leg and then move it into place followed by gently pressing down on the awning while the adhesive takes hold. Do this for each leg, one at a time until you have secured all three back-side legs followed by all three front-side legs. The roof supports The left-side roof support beam fits within the notch at the top of the left-side wall and the beam support shelf of the middle wall. Once in position, make sure that the beam is sitting flush with the surfaces of the middle wall support shelf and the inside of the left-wall. The right-side clerestory sub-assembly also serves as the roof support beam for the main right-side roof sections. Apply adhesive to both ends where indicated and position the beam structure between the notches of the right-side front and back walls. Key to this step is making sure that the clesestory sub-assembly is sitting level/balanced between the walls … you should be able to judge it being level by observing how the roof support surfaces align evenly with the top edges of the walls on both sides. The roof sections For the left-side roof sections, note that the underside of each roof panel there are recessed areas that are intended to be positioned over the top edges of the walls being covered … there is no need to specifically align these recesses as the alignment of the roof sections are more dependent on getting the top edges of the roof panels snugly positioned under the beam's top finished surface as seen in the final image of this illustration. On the right side of our factory, the two main roof sections are designed to fit around the clerestory with the main roof section that has the factory chimney being mounted on the far right side. Take care to not damage the chimney when attaching that roof section. Again, take care to align the top edges of each roof section to fit snugly just “under” the top surface of the beam. Finally, attach the remaining small roof sections to the top of the clerestory structure. Some final details The left-side chimney needs to be installed using a little bit of adhesive … make sure that the lower angled surface of the chimney sits flush with the exposed portion of the beam such that the chimney sits vertical on the roof. All that remains now are the shipping crates and the utility cabinet. You can see where I've chosen to position the utility cabinet on the side of the factory, using a small dot of adhesive on the upper back of the cabinet to hold it against the wall. Shipping crate placement is up to you … here are a couple of examples where the crates have been left on the trackside dock. I hope that copies of this model find good homes on model train layouts around the world … if you are careful and patient, you should be able to produce a nice looking structure … have fun with it!

more sizes will be available soon / if demand is good :) After looking at normal paintbrushes and thinking, “surely a 3D printer could make one of these,” I ended up making this fully 3D printed working paintbrush. The full brush can print in under 40 minutes , and the best part is that the bristles are replaceable. So if they get too worn, bent, clogged up, or abused during a project, you can just print a fresh set of bristles instead of binning the whole brush. The bristle section is designed to be folded at the 43 mm point so it fits snugly into the brush head. Once fitted, the bristles stick out around 60 mm , but this is very customizable. You can cut them shorter, trim them into shape, or stiffen/soften the feel depending on what you want to use it for. The full brush is around 150 mm long , with the red handle section being roughly 75 mm , making it a short, comfortable, quick-use brush rather than a big chunky tool. This started as a fun “can this be done?” 3D printing idea, but it is actually useful. It could be used as: A quick emergency paintbrush A dusting brush A delicate cleaning brush A model-making brush A small archaeology/excavation-style brush A workshop brush for loose dust or debris Or whatever random use you find for it check oit the pics for assembly help The idea is simple: imagine being somewhere with a 3D printer but no brush. A workshop, research facility, maker space, garage, classroom, campsite, or just your house at midnight when you suddenly need to paint something. Print this, fold the bristles, slot them in, and you have a working brush. No AMS is needed. It can be printed as separate colour parts, or all in one colour if you just want the fastest functional version. Print / Assembly Notes Bristle fold point: 43 mm Bristle length sticking out: around 60 mm Full brush length: around 150 mm Handle grip length: around 75 mm Print time: under 40 minutes AMS: not required To assemble, fold the bristle part at the 43 mm point and fit it snugly into the brush head. You can then trim the bristles to whatever length or stiffness works best for your use. P.S. When folding the bristle part, make sure you fold the shorter end first. One side is longer than the other, and if the longer side is folded the wrong way, it will not fit into the brush head properly. The silver/metal-looking part has been made with general printer tolerances in mind, so depending on your printer, the fit onto the red handle may be slightly loose. A small dab of glue on the inside of the silver part may be needed to hold it securely to the red handle. Once that part is fixed in place, the bristles are still removable and replaceable. Just pull the used bristle section out and fit a fresh one in. You can also trim the bristles to suit your needs — shorter for a stiffer brush, longer for a softer/flickier action.

description: Schedule 40 PVC pipe coupler with a female slip end and a female NPT threaded end. This PVC coupler adapts standard slip-fit PVC pipe to threaded fittings, hoses, or valves — no glue required on the threaded side. This parametric PVC coupler bridges two of the most common pipe connection types in one printed part: a smooth slip socket sized to standard Schedule 40 PVC pipe, and a true NPT (National Pipe Thread) female thread on the opposite end, cut to ASME B1.20.1 tapered thread specifications for a proper mechanical seal with threaded male fittings. I created an all‑direction protector for TinyWhoop. It is available in two sizes: a 130 mm type and a 160 mm type. By mounting this 360° protector parallel and level to the aircraft’s center axis, acro‑mode flight becomes possible. Because the weight increases, the operating difficulty becomes slightly higher, but since the guard is installed, I believe the likelihood of damage is reduced. The structure has moderate flexibility, helping protect the FC and the frame. It can also run along the ground. The weight is approximately 16 g for the 130 mm type and about 20 g for the 160 mm type, so it is recommended for use with 0802 motors or larger. Print Parts 1–3 in PETG, and Parts 4–5 in TPU. For assembly, 3 mm acrylic rods are required, which can be purchased inexpensively at home improvement stores. For the 130 mm type, use six rods cut to about 75–80 mm and one rod cut to about 130 mm. For the 160 mm type, use six rods cut to 100 mm and one rod cut to 160 mm. Adjust the lengths as needed depending on the six rods placed around the circumference. Please make sure the six rods around the circumference are all the same length. After forming the circular shape with these six rods, determine the final length of the center acrylic rod. Cut the center rod slightly longer at first, then trim off the excess after test‑fitting to avoid mistakes. After printing the parts, the protector can be assembled by simply snapping the pieces together. Parts 3 are mounted to the canopy.Secure them with cable ties and insert the center acrylic rod through the cut‑out center section. Instead of Parts3, you can also drill a 3.5 mm hole in the genuine C03 canopy and use it that way (see photo 15).This one was more stable. Parts 5 function as a stopper to keep the aircraft centered.Please leave a slight gap between Parts 3 and Parts 5. The alignment may shift due to crash impacts. Adjust the horizontal alignment using Parts 3, and fine‑tune the front‑rear tilt by changing the battery position. The 130 mm type is intended for 65‑size frames, and the 160 mm type is intended for 75‑size frames. However, by adjusting the length of the acrylic rods, a 75‑size frame should also fit in the 130 mm type. After connecting the side parts with the six round rods arranged around the circumference and assembling them into a spherical shape, insert the aircraft through the gaps between the pillars and then attach the center shaft. Sufficient space is provided for easy access to the battery as well. If you have any questions, feel free to leave a comment. (Added on July 12, 2026) Additional types of mount parts for the canopy are planned to be added in the future. (Added on July 13, 2026) I have added an explanation to the description regarding using the genuine C03 canopy by drilling a 3.5 mm hole (in this case, Parts3 is not used). Meet Wheely , probably the cutest little starter robot you'll print this week. It’s designed to be super beginner-friendly, making it a perfect weekend project to get into robotics without the usual wiring headaches. This project is a mashup of a few designs I love. It’s a remix that combines the modularity and style of CUBY , the fun community spirit of Otto DIY , and some clever mechanical ideas from Winchy . Weekend project You won't need to waste days of printing time or a whole spool of filament for this one. It's an incredibly optimized print that only uses 82 grams of filament! In just 3 hours and 44 minutes you will be building the robot ready to start playing. Servos For the wheels you will need 2x 9g Continuous Rotation Digital Servo-360°. Instead of using standard DC motors I decided to build Wheely around servo motors. Servos are way easier to wire up, plug in, and program. If you are just starting out or building this with kids, this setup will save you a lot of frustration. The Remote Control: The controller layout is very intuitive. Each joystick directly controls one servo, giving you easy, tank-like steering control. Speed & Power: In the default code, I have programmed the servos to run at 50% power. This keeps the movements smooth, quiet, and perfect for driving around a desk. However, if you want more speed, you can easily modify the code to unleash 100% of their power. Controller and control scheme At this moment you can use the CyberBrick Official Standard Remote or other controller that uses the same wiring.

description: This model is the third in a series of “Thinline Scale Model” structure kits for Z-scale and N-scale model railroading. [Note: the HO-scale version of this kit is available here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/3036818-the-trackside-factory-ho-scale-edition#profileId-3414170 .] The Trackside Factory (TSM#03) - This structure kit is for a factory that could be located off of a track siding. For my layout, this factory will be receiving lumber from a lumber mill down the line and producing wood-based products, such as furniture, for shipping out to market via the railroad. To see other kits in this series, including HO-scale versions, please visit my collection page: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/15297762-model-train-projects . I designed this model in SolidWorks inspired by an original design by a former member of our Z-scale modeling club - he did market a laser-cut wood kit for a short while (as fannocreek designs ) but alas those kits are no longer available so he graciously gave me permission to craft my model as a likeness of his . Given my model is for 3d-printing, I've completely re-engineered the way that the kit is made and assembled, and I've made other design changes based on how some interior aspects of the factory would change some of the exterior appearance. And, after many failed attempts to recreate an exposed support structure under the trackside dock and front deck that would print reliably in one piece, I chose to enclose the underside of both dock and deck. Important Note: Before proceeding to print and build these kits, please note the following special requirements needed to produce good results. Also, please read through the entire description to understand all of the assembly steps required. For printing, a 0.2mm nozzle and a clean smooth build plate is required - this model is specifically designed for using a 0.08mm layer layer height and a 0.22mm line width for the Z-scale model. The N-scale model uses a 0.11mm layer height and a 0.22mm line width. This kit includes both two-color and three-color prints - an AMS is required. Supplied needed: fast setting (5-10 seconds) CA adhesive with a toothpick or tool for spreading along mating edges; and a selection of acrylic paints / brushes for painting the model (if desired). Tools needed: a good bed scraper tool for removing some of parts from the smooth build plate - I found the bed scraping blade supplied with the printers by Bambu Lab to work well for this purpose (most beneficial was its thin sharp blade for lifting very thin prints) . The Print Profiles - Three profiles each are available for each model train scale ( Z or N ) of this structure kit, the profiles generally differ by single ( P1S , A1 , H2S , etc.) and dual-nozzle ( H2D and H2C ) printers, and also an A1 Mini -specific profile. Please note that all of the profiles include a number of parameter changes from the standard print profiles that probably should not be tampered with if you want good results. One of the more important profile variances is that I've significantly slowed down the nozzle speed, travel speed and acceleration to help assure the best result printing the detail features of these models - I've specifically supplied separate profiles based on direct-drive nozzle count because changing the printer of a single-nozzle profile to a dual-nozzle printer (and vice versa) may cause the speed settings to be lost in the profile. I highly recommend that you use the appropriate single or dual-nozzle profile matching your printer capability, and I include the X2D with the single-nozzle printers since its auxiliary nozzle is not recommended for use with a 0.2mm nozzle . Important note regarding the factory name: The original laser-cut wood kit included decals for naming the factory, a choice of either “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” or “ TELLER & SONS MFG ”, the latter one being the one I'm planning to use on my Z-scale layout. For the Z-scale profiles, I've only included the “ TELLER & SONS MFG ” choice as the other name is too long to print cleanly. For the N-scale profiles, I've included both naming options with the “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” as the default choice - if you prefer “ TELLER & SONS MFG ” on your N-scale model, find the build plate where the wall with the name appears and deselect the named wall you don't want and select the named wall that you do want. Make sure that only one of these walls are selected for printing … if both are selected, Bambu Studio should complain and you will need to deselect one to proceed; if none are selected, you will be missing a wall in the print so make that one is selected. If you have questions about any of this, please feel free to reach out to me. One final note … you can optionally remove the name from the wall by deleting the text element, or you can attempt to change the name to something you prefer but please note that you should take care to recenter, left to right, the text on the wall after you edit the name. Also note that the text tool when used on a textured surface such as these walls can be a bit finicky with sometimes distorting the placement of individual characters so you might have to mess around with it a bit to get it to behave. I've taken some care to make sure that the text fits nicely when positioned vertically across the siding boards. And finally, most of the text fonts available will not print well at these scales which is why I've focused on the two sans-serif fonts used in the profile. Important note before removing the parts from the build plate: After printing your model, please only remove the parts after the build plate has completely cooled to room temperature. Many of the model parts are extremely thin (e.g., between 0.64 and 0.8mm in Z-scale ) and can be easily damaged. Some of the parts can't be removed simply by flexing the build plate so with the build plate removed from the printer and set firmly on a work surface, use a sharp bed scraper tool to very carefully work up and lift each individual part by working slowly around the edges of the part. When removing some of the smaller parts, such as the L-shaped awning supports, you may want to place your hand over to capture them as they will tend to fly off once released from the plate. Choosing Filaments - In my profiles, I've chosen to use Bambu Lab PLA Matte filaments as I prefer the surface finish over PLA Basic . With the model based on four colors as set in the profiles, all of the major elements of the model could be left as printed but there are a small number of details that I recommend be painted to help finish the model (see below for painting recommendations). I've tried to minimize the number of color changes needed on each build plate in the profiles to keep purge waste as low as possible. === ASSEMBLY INSTRUCTIONS === This diagram provides a general overview of the kit parts. The Z-scale and N-scale kits have the same set of parts - in terms of design, only the two small winch supports differ between the kits as the detail of the N-scale supports could not be reliably replicated in Z-scale. While these instructions are illustrated with pictures of the N-scale kit, the instructions are the same for the Z-scale kit. === Painting and Window Glazing Recommendations === At a minimum, I would suggest adding some diluted color washes to give a more weathered look to the structure. Before assembling the kits in the photos, I choose to paint the lower masonry block surfaces of the two white bases to help bring out the detail. I first coated the masonry surfaces with a white acrylic gesso and after that dried thoroughly, I worked it over with a thinned coat of ‘tarnished’ black, the gesso helps to create a more receptive surface for the paint on the plastic. For those interested, here is an Amazon link to the Micro-Mark Acrylic paints I've used on my models: https://a.co/d/0fMC2PB2 . There are a number of details in this kit that should be painted prior to assembly. This include the two chimneys, the utility cabinet, the shipping crates, and the firebox as seem in the following photo. The firebox is an integrated feature of the middle wall and it takes a bit of extra care in painting it without getting paint on the wall siding (blue) - note that I chose to paint the lid in gray with the rest of the box in red. For the crates, I only chose to dirty them up a bit to help differentiate them from the dock color. Note: If you choose to change the filament colors to either reduce the number of filaments or simply to picking more neutral colors with a plan of painting the model, you should consider painting individual parts prior to assembly although adding weathering detail is often done with the overall model built up. Using some paint color washes can help enhance the details while also making the building not appear as it was just build yesterday :-). If you want to add window glazing (simulated window glass), I would suggest that being done either before attaching the walls to the base, or at least right after attaching the walls to the base - going beyond those steps in the assembly process will make it difficult to adding glazing. You also need to consider that if you are painting the model, care must be taken to not get paint on your window glazing so the painting versus glazing order becomes important. I'm still messing around with different techniques for glazing 3d-printed models … either using a clear film/plastic material or something like this clear adhesive by Microscale Industries ( https://a.co/d/0gy3e33L ) that can also be used to form small windows on models (this stuff can be a bit tricky to get it to work right but I've successfully used similar, unfortunately discontinued by Micro-Mark , products in the past. === Starting with some sub-assemblies === There are a number of sub-assemblies to complete prior to starting the general assembly of the kit. It is recommended that before applying adhesive, you study all of the photos closely to see how parts are supposed to fit once assembled. Once each is completed, set it aside until needed in the general assembly. The Fire Escape Note the alignment of the underside notches of the ladder to the support features of the wall - make sure to get the ladder in the proper orientation with the shorter piece of the ladder above the top notch and the longer piece of the ladder below the bottom notch (and extending below the wall once attached. Also take care to center the latter, left to right, on the provided supports. This can be a rather delicate job and using some tweezers might be helpful. Note the alignment of the escape platform with the two provided wall supports centered beween the platform leg structures. The Winch Support Beams The winch supports are two small parts that look somewhat like mini-tripods. Note the alignment of the winch support relative to the top of the door and the notch in the wall. The awning platforms with supports Note that the support legs have bumps that fit into the underside slots of the awning bases. Also note that the leg of the support is positioned closest to the thinner edge of the awning base. Key to this sub-assembly is to make sure that the supports sit flush against the surface of the base with the leg standing straight up, left to right, from the base. The larger awning platform is for the trackside dock and the smaller one is for the front deck. The clerestory Note that the four walls fit well within the inside cavity of the main roof beam base. Once they are in position with all of the wall edges lined up and with the walls firmly seated down within the cavity, add the adhesive drops where the walls meet and with a couple more at the base on the longer walls down where they meet the base, and hold everything in position, making sure not to disrupt that the wall edges appear properly aligned with no obvious gaps. The upper beam can then be added with adhesive on the small flat surfaces of the beam to glue to the inside of the end walls when set into the alignment gaps. The right-side chimney Note that the chimney needs to be inserted from the underside of the roof section and oriented with the thicker side of the chimney wedge base positioned toward the large gap side of the roof. Once you have the chimney firmly seated flush to the underside of the roof, apply some adhesive to hold it in place. The chimney wedged base serves to orient the chimney vertical once the roof is installed on the model. Now you should have the following sub-assemblies ready for use when starting the general assembly of the factory. === Assembling the factory === The base Each of the interlocking tabs on the left-side base, the trackside dock and the front deck have corresponding receiving slots on the right-side base, and for the dock and deck, also on the left-side base. Gently press each tab into its corresponding slot and work each in until its fully inserted and flush … it helps to place the assembly on a solid surface and press things down from the top but be careful to not damage any of the other features on the bases when doing this … I've strengthened the underside of the bases in the areas around the slots to facilitate pressing down in those areas. While these four parts are designed to hold together without need for gluing, you may choose to add some CA adhesive to the mating joints underneath once the parts are mated up flush together. The right-side walls Start with the middle wall … note the alignment notch position where the middle should lock into place. Make sure that the wall sits flush with the side of the stairway and other vertical features of the base. Next is the back wall … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and a mid-point along the bottom edge … if all goes according to plan, once in place, the edge between the middle and back walls should line up very nicely. Continue with the front wall … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and a mid-point along the bottom edge. Next is installing the second floor insert … note the orientation of the second floor insert and how it aligns at the top of the stairway. Apply adhesive drops at the tops of the vertical features of the base and then place the second floor insert within the structure and flush down on those features. After the floor is in place, you may choose to add some more adhesive to help secure the front and back walls to the second floor. Finally, adding the right-side wall sub-assembly with the fire escape … take care not to damage the ladder when handling this wall section. Again, apply small adhesive drops to the exposed surfaces where the wall will sit. The left-side walls Starting with the back wall, apply small adhesive drops where shown and assure that the wall is flush with the base alignment edge and vertical features once in place. Next, add the front wall ... Finally, add the left-side wall using the vertical surface of the fireplace feature for adhesive and as a supporting surface for the wall. The awnings Each awning sub-assembly has three slots that are designed to align with the three support tabs on the left-side front and back walls. To install each awning sub-assembly, gently press the slots over the corresponding tabs … make sure to not damage the awning support legs while doing this. I generally start with one of the end slots followed by the opposite end slot, making sure that the middle slot is in its proper place as I press them together. Place a finger inside the wall as support while pressing the awning base flush to the outside of the wall. No adhesive is needed at this point. Repeat with the awning against the back wall. Make sure that the awning bases are flush with the walls before proceeding … it may take some persuasion but do be careful to not damage anything while working them on. Now is time to install the awning top surfaces. Examine the awning surface parts closely … note that one of the long edges of each will have a complete shingle row and the other a partial one, the partial row should end up mounted close to the wall so that the complete row of shingles is exposed along the outer edge of the awning. Apply adhesive drops along the edges close to the wall and the outside edge of the awning. (If, as you move the awning surface pieces into place, a bit of adhesive gets pushed up into the crack where the awning base is pressed against the wall, that would not be a bad thing :o). Now it is time to add some adhesive to keep the awning legs in the proper place … for this, you will need either a toothpick or another way to gab a small drop of adhesive behind each of the legs where they will sit up against the leg alignment features of the dock and deck. Each leg should be positioned in front of and centered on each alignment bump … the legs are a bit flexible and move easily at this point so dab on a small drop of adhesive just behind the lower back portion of the leg and then move it into place followed by gently pressing down on the awning while the adhesive takes hold. Do this for each leg, one at a time until you have secured all three back-side legs followed by all three front-side legs. The roof support beams The left-side roof support beam fits within the notch at the top of the left-side wall and the beam support shelf of the middle wall. Once in position, make sure that the beam is sitting flush with the surfaces of the middle wall support shelf and the inside of the left-wall. The right-side clerestory sub-assembly also serves as the roof support beam for the main right-side roof sections. Apply adhesive to both ends where indicated and position the beam structure between the notches of the right-side front and back walls. Key to this step is making sure that the clesestory sub-assembly is sitting level/balanced between the walls … you should be able to judge it being level by observing how the roof support surfaces align evenly with the top edges of the walls on both sides. The roof sections For the left-side roof sections, note that the underside of each roof panel there are recessed areas that are intended to be positioned over the top edges of the walls being covered … there is no need to specifically align these recesses as the alignment of the roof sections are more dependent on getting the top edges of the roof panels snugly positioned under the beam's top finished surface as seen in the final image of this illustration. On the right side of our factory, the two main roof sections are designed to fit around the clerestory with the main roof section that has the factory chimney being mounted on the far right side. Take care to not damage the chimney when attaching that roof section. Finally, attach the remaining small roof sections to the top of the clerestory structure. Some final details The left-side chimney needs to be installed using a little bit of adhesive … make sure that the lower angled surface of the chimney sits flush with the exposed portion of the beam such that the chimney sits vertical on the roof. All that remains now are the shipping crates and the utility cabinet. You can see where I've chosen to position the utility cabinet on the side of the factory, using a small dot of adhesive on the upper back of the cabinet to hold it against the wall. Shipping crate placement is up to you … here are a couple of examples where the crates have been left on the trackside dock. I hope that copies of this model find good homes on model train layouts around the world … I have a spot on my Z-scale layout where Teller & Sons Manufacturing will definitely be doing business … if you are careful and patient, you should be able to produce a nice looking structure … have fun with it!

Features Filament Zero is designed to save you money and time: Impossibly light & fast: not 0.1g more than absolutely necessary & it'll be done before you notice it started Choose from 3 strength options: flexible Net, semi-rigid Tape and rigid Beam Sparse Gridfinity - beyond impossibly light & fast: halve your print time and filament again with sparse baseplates Filament Zero lets you create any gridfinity layout you need effortlessly: Interlocking: strong baseplate interlocking system Any Custom Grid Size: set any width and length (half-unit increments) Built-In, Custom Drawer Spacers: add drawer-fit spacers to any side (mm increments) Any Custom Shape: Ls, circles, triangles, etc… Powerful Multi Baseplate Generator: all the plates you need to cover any area in one click Note: Filament Zero does not support magnets. Four Filament Zero Models Filament Zero comes in four models to meet all your baseplate needs. There are trade-offs between model weight and model strength. During design, I realized there were three main tradeoff points for various use cases. Rather than making one model to meet everybody's needs, I made three main models to address the three main optimal weight strength trade-offs. The fourth model, FZBeam+ is an interlocking vs aesthetics & time trade-off. FZ Model Quick Selection Guide There are two main decisions you need to make to choose your model: Strength? How rigid and strong do you need your baseplates to be? Flexible : FZNet+ (lightest) X-Y rigid : FZTape+ (balanced) X-Y-Z rigid : FZBeam / FZBeam+ (strongest) Interlocking? Do you prefer to have your baseplates fully interlocked? The “+” in the model name indicates interlocking. Yes: FZNet+ , FZTape+ or FZBeam+ No: FZNet+ , FZTape+ or FZBeam About the Models FZ Net+ (lightest, flexible) — Think fisherman's net. Choose this if you want the lightest, fastest option and you are going to fully fill your grid with bins. The primary structural requirement for baseplates is to hold your bins together. Net does exactly that and nothing more… at 190 tiles per hour and 7,500 tiles per kilogram . Nearly 2x the tiles per kilogram and 2.7x the tiles per hour of the lightest base on MakerWorld, of any kind. FZ Tape+ (optimal, X-Y rigid) — Semi-rigid: rigid in the X/Y plane when placed on a flat surface, flexible in Z. The best overall performance. Strong in all the ways that matter yet still unbelievably fast and lightweight to print. It's in the same weight class as the best flexible base on MakerWorld, yet is strong and prints 1.5x faster . FZ Beam (strongest, X-Y-Z rigid) — Fully rigid, strong and the most like classic gridfinity-like styling. To me, this is the most aesthetically pleasing lightweight model anywhere while also being the most efficient rigid base on MakerWorld: 1.7x more tiles per kilogram and 1.5x more tiles per hour than the previous rigid record holder. FZ Beam+ (FZ Beam + Interlocking) – For slightly more print time, but about the same weight, you can print FZ-Beam plates with full interlocking capabilities. How strong does a baseplate actually need to be? Step back and ask what a gridfinity baseplate actually does: it holds your bins in place. Once bins are seated and the plate is resting on a flat surface, the surface provides all the vertical support. Gravity holds everything down. The only job left for the baseplate is resisting horizontal forces: keeping bins from sliding apart when you push, pull, and rummage. Structurally, that's a tension-and-shear problem in the plane of the plate, not a stiffness problem. That insight is what makes the three regimes possible: Net takes the insight to its logical conclusion. Like a fisherman's net, it only resists tension. On a flat surface with bins seated, that's genuinely all you need, and it's why Net can be so radically light. The trade-off: it has essentially no rigidity of its own. It's a conforming skeleton, not a structure. Handle it empty and it flops; that's the point. Tape adds in-plane rigidity. Sitting on a flat surface, it's rigid in X and Y: bins stay locked in their grid, and the plate keeps its shape as you load and unload. It still flexes in Z, so it conforms to slightly uneven surfaces and pops out of drawers easily. For most real-world use, this is the sweet spot: everything a baseplate must do rigidly, it does rigidly. Beam is rigid in all directions, the classical gridfinity experience. It resists twisting and bending even when picked up and feels like a solid foundation in the hand. If you move plates around with bins on them, or your surface isn't flat, or you simply want the familiar feel, Beam is the one, and it's still lighter and faster than any other rigid base on MakerWorld. The progression is simple: each step up adds rigidity in a new direction, and costs filament and time. Pick the regime that matches how you actually use your grid. Aesthetics (for the few seconds you'll see it) Let's be honest: a baseplate spends its life hidden under bins. Once your grid is loaded, you'll never see it. So Net and Tape make no apologies for looking like what they are: pure function, though beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Beam is the exception. Its strength comes from triangles, arranged to maximize strength per gram as printed, and a key innovation was removing all the rounded, extended parts of the original gridfinity profile: they serve no mechanical purpose and dramatically slow down printing. What's left is a faceted, multi-triangle surface that looks almost prismatic. The goal was always strength per weight; the looks are what optimization happens to look like. The Interlock System Need your baseplates locked together? No sliding, no drifting — a single unified grid before a single bin goes down. We've got you covered. The system itself was a happy accident. In stripping out every gram of unnecessary filament, the corners emptied out since the bins never touch them. That empty corner space turned out to be the natural home for an interlocking cap. Net and Tape became interlocking the moment I designed the cap; the only real work was creating Beam+, the interlocking variant of Beam. The result: small caps that snap into the corners where plates meet, resisting both tension and shear. They print in minutes by the dozen, and every interlocking plate is compatible with every other, so you can mix and match Net+, Tape+, and Beam+ freely in one locked grid. Interlocks also unlock more advanced custom shapes: while the customizer handles basic shapes like Ls, circles, triangles etc, shapes with a holes or a complex perimeters may need to be printed in two or more pieces. The interlock system then lets you connect those parts together to form a solid whole. Filament Zero Performance Weight: Filament is Money How much filament do you need to complete your Gridfinity baseplate job? One way to answer that is to figure out the average weight per tile for a particular gridfinity base plate. Filament Zero is so light, though. (down to 0.133g/tile ), that it's hard to compare this way. Instead, I've started comparing models by how many tiles can you get out of a kilogram of filament: Tiles per Kilogram or TpKG. Speed: Time is our most precious resource I don't know about you, but I hate waiting for 3D prints to complete. To me, print speed is even more important than filament use, though the two go hand in hand. Though I aggressively optimized every print profile, I did not change the print speed settings. That means you can probably use Sport Mode or even Ludacris Mode to print these in even less time (not tested!). However, These models already print so fast that the final print time is dominated by the printer's prep time. Nobody's is. The whole point of gridfinity is a system that fits your space — and stock rectangular baseplates almost never do. The customizer is where Filament Zero goes from "efficient baseplate" to "the exact baseplate your drawer has been waiting for": any size, half-unit precision, spacers for a perfect friction fit, custom shapes for odd corners, even auto-generated plate sets for big areas. Beginner Customization Guide: Pick a model, Pick a size → Download & Print Start Customizing: Click “Customize” below the print profiles Select the “Single Baseplate” option Look for the customization options in the Customize panel, usually on the left. Pick your Filament Zero Model: In the Customize panel, the Model dropdown chooses which base style to build: Beam — rigid, classic feel (choose Beam+ if you plan to interlock multiple plates) Tape+ — semi-rigid: holds bins firmly, flexes to lift out of drawers Net+ — ultralight and flexible: absolute minimum filament and print time Set your size: Under Grid , set columns (squares wide) and rows (squares deep). A gridfinity square is 42mm, so a 4x4 plate is 168x168mm. Generate: Click “Generate” and after few moments, you'll see your model in the preview. Download: See the Download and Print Guide below That's it. A custom-sized baseplate in under a minute, no modeling required. Parametric Model Maker Download & Print Guide Question: “Why are my custom FZ prints way slower and use way more filament than claimed?” Answer: The MakerWorld Parametric Model Maker doesn't support all the print-profile controls Filament Zero needs. Here's how to use the customizer AND get FZ's full performance: Customize & Export you Filament Zero Baseplate(s) as STL Customize as you like (Beginner Customization Guide above or Features Guide below) Click Download (top right) When it asks for 3MF vs STL: Select STL! Download and Open Matching Filament Zero Base Print Profile On this page, select one of the base profiles that match your model choice (Net+, Tape+, Beam or Beam+) Click “open in Bambu studio” to download and open it. Delete the existing objects (Edit → Delete All) Set the Printer to match your Printer Save (optional): You can re-use this file and skip Step 2 in the future. Import your Custom STL into the optimized Filament Zero Print Profile Add in your custom STL (File → Import → STL - or just drag the file into Bambu Studio) IMPORTANT if your STL has more than one baseplate: Click the “Split to Objects” icon (with your STL selected) then press “A” to auto-arrange objects across all plates (see Multi Baseplate Print Prep below) NOW you can print with maximum efficiency. I wish this was easer. You should be able to just download the 3MF and have it work perfectly. I'll be petitioning MakerWorld to better support advanced 3MF print profiles in the Parametric Model Maker. Features Guide Sparse Gridfinity Bigger project? Bigger savings. Sparse mode removes inner geometry, creating 84x84mm cells wherever they fit — halving material and doubling print speed on top of everything above. For larger gridfinity layouts, and especially larger trays, this is all you need. Net+ in sparse mode approaches 20,000 standard squares per kilogram and nearly 500 squares per hour . But the sweet spot is Tape+ at 7,692/kg and 271/h: the extra rigidity is the right compromise for a sparse layout while keeping incredible efficiency. Run a few test prints and experiment with your layout. And nobody likes printing separate spacers that pop out, drift, and rattle either. Print your spacers as part of your baseplate : add them to any of the four sides, in 1mm increments, for a snug fit that locks your whole grid in place. Add spacers to any side in MM increments Custom Shapes Drawers aren't always rectangles. Corners, notches, angled walls — real spaces have odd shapes, and your baseplate should fit them. Remove squares from the left and right of any row, in any configuration, to create nearly any shape you need. And if the shape configurator can't do it, split it in two: print two plates and join them with the interlock system. Instead of counting gridfinity squares, just enter your layout's width and depth in millimeters and Filament Zero generates exactly the baseplates you need. Pick your printer from the list and it automatically knows your build plate size — so usually it's just: pick your printer, pick your model, set your area, go. Fine-tuning options are there when you need them. Filament Zero already saves you printer time; this saves your time too, and if you're printing a lot of gridfinity, total time saved is what actually matters. Automatically generate all the plates you need for your area. Just specify the width and depth in MM, FZ takes care of the rest. WLED Remote+ - WLED Remote & HomeKit Bridge A standalone ESP32-S3 controller for WLED that combines a physical remote UI with a HomeKit bridge on a LilyGo T-Display S3. The project provides local hardware controls, WLED discovery and control over the network, and Apple Home integration in a single device. Features Physical remote interface with the built-in display, left/right buttons, and rotary encoder on the LilyGo T-Display S3 hardware. WLED discovery on the local network using mDNS plus direct control through the WLED JSON API. HomeKit bridge support via HomeSpan, exposing WLED as a light plus preset switches for Apple Home. Captive-portal Wi-Fi onboarding with fallback configuration flow and persistent settings stored in NVS. Embedded local configuration web UI served on port 8080 for setup, discovery, status, and reset actions. Built with PlatformIO for the lilygo-t-display-s3 environment and Arduino framework on ESP32. Hardware The target device is a LilyGo T-Display S3 with ESP32-S3, PSRAM, a 170x320 ST7789 display, two front buttons, and a rotary encoder used for navigation and control. The display stack is driven with LovyanGFX, and the project also depends on WiFiManager, HomeSpan, and ArduinoJson. Setup Flash the firmware to the board and boot it. Connect the device to Wi-Fi using the built-in WiFiManager flow; if saved credentials fail, it falls back to a captive portal for setup. Discover a WLED instance on the local network or configure the WLED host manually through the local config UI. Open the configuration page on port 8080 to review status, scan for devices, save settings, or reset configuration. Pair the device with Apple Home using the HomeKit QR flow shown by the UI when HomeKit is enabled. HomeKit behavior The HomeKit bridge exposes one light bulb accessory with On, Brightness, Hue, and Saturation characteristics, plus up to eight switch accessories that trigger WLED presets.[cite:2] The project overview also notes a default HomeKit setup code of 46637726, and the firmware can generate an X-HM:// pairing URI for QR-based setup. WLED integration The firmware talks to WLED over HTTP using endpoints such as /json/state, /json/effects, and /json/presets, and it posts state updates back to /json/state for actions like power, brightness, color, effect, and preset selection. WLED instances are discovered over mDNS using the _wled._tcp service, which keeps first-time configuration simple on a local network. AI assistance This project was developed with the help of AI-assisted tooling for planning, code generation, refactoring, and documentation support. Depending on the Task, different Technologies whre used. Mostly QWEN and GEMMA Models through ollama, but also cloud Models like Claude Opus were used. There are quite some files in this repository to guide AI Agents into writing better code and not making too many mistakes. You can use them as a guideline for your own project. Web installer Flash the latest firmware from the browser through GitHub Pages: Open the WLEDRemote+ installer . License This project is licensed under the MIT License . See LICENSE for the full text. description: This is a compact folding drone platform to give your drone a flat surface to take off from or land on. They can also be used for marking for surveys or even as a simple fold-able tray. It can be customized for the exact size you want/need it to be. Using the Makerworld Parametric Model Maker Click the “Customize” button above then click “Customize” again and it will bring you to the Makerworld Parametric Model Maker. To customize this model for you: Change the “Plate Width” to the width you want the plate to be. If you are fitting this into a case use the space you have available minus about 2mm so if you have 170mm available make it 168mm. Remember this is for each individual plate which is the size when folded. The actual plate size unfolded will be double this. Change the “Plate Length” to the length you want the plate to be. This needs a little extra space for the hinges so minus 2mm and the plate height below. So if have 130mm available subtract plate height (4.5mm) + 2mm buffer gets you to 123.5mm. Change the "Plate Height" if needed. Try to stay to a 4.5mm minimum. This one shouldn't need much extra clearance as the plate folds pretty flat but add a 1mm - 2mm buffer just in case. So if your space is 20mm the height can go up to 4.75mm (4.75mm x 4 main plates = 19mm + 1mm buffer). For standard pieces of filament used for the hinges leave the bore as 1.05mm. All the hinges are offset plate to plate by 0.1mm like a slight zigzag so at 1.05mm radius the effective diameter is actually 2.0mm even (1.05mm * 2mm = 2.1mm minus the 0.1mm offset). This seems to be the best value for this where the bores aren't to tight to get filament in but also not too loose where it falls out. The drop down for “Which Part” you want to create will default to “Everything” which is usually what you want. If you changed the sizes above click “Generate” to refresh the model. Click “Download” then select your printer and click “Confirm”. Click “Download” again and select a 3MF file then when prompted save the file. Open the file in Bambu Studio, right click the model, and select “Split → To Objects”. Add some additional print plates to your model then move each folding plate to its own with Plate 5 (the thin one) on a plate with the clips. Make sure to right click and “Auto Rotate” each plate which will put everything into the best orientations with the hinges up and the face of the plate down. Turn on support, set your default profile (I recommend 0.20 High Quality), for a bit of extra sturdiness set the walls to 3 or 4, and print. Download a Premade Model There are currently three different types of premade models if you don't want to use the generator. description: fix for subaru crosstrek / subaru impreza cup holder. Cup holder insert that secures drinks better. I have had my car for many years, and for all that time I have disliked the cup holder design. for some reason it isnt complete circles, and has a bunch of extra room that leads to most beverage containers to be so loose, that as you turn, start, and stop, its got a high chance of tipping. Finally I had one spill to many and started looking for commercially available solutions. I decided that with a little bit of work, I could design my own cup holder insert that fixes my issues and fits great. Took me longer than I would have liked, but im excited to share the result of this work. A bit about my solution: So for starters, This model was designed for use with PETG or other material that will not warp or degrade from the sun and heat its surely to be constantly subjected to. The insert fits great in my cup holder, a 2020 Subaru Crosstrek. I'm certain it fits the 2018-2021 models for sure, you'll have to confirm for sure if it fits in other years. I'm sure it fits in the Impreza as well, as the interiors are the same. The insert is held in just by the taper of the cup holder, and it seems to secure it great, yet allow easy removal for when you do need the larger size opening. I designed it to start a bit above the bottom of the cup holder, to allow for cup holder inserts you might be using, and the small gap at the bottom makes it easy to remove by grabbing it in the gap at the bottom. The top of the insert falls just below the divider in between cup holders, and includes the opening for handles. I kept it at a height to roll into the radius of the cup holder, and the rim of the insert matches up to just below the trim of the cars cup holder opening. The holder can be used in the front or back position and fits the same in either. Personally I like to use it in only my back cup holder, leaving the larger front to place items or larger drinks like Gatoraid bottles. I tested and made many revisions in the sizing to get to the current design that im sharing. model_name: Eclipse Putter - Low Torque / Modular / High MOI
description: Eclipse - A Modular High-MOI 3D Printed Putter Looking for a customizable putter without the price tag of today's premium designs? This project combines the flexibility of 3D printing with design features inspired by modern high-performance putters. The putter head is designed to incorporate removable weights, allowing the majority of the mass to be positioned around the perimeter. This increases the moment of inertia (MOI), helping improve stability on off-center strikes while reducing twisting through impact. One of the key features of this design is its modular construction. The shaft insert is a separate component that bolts into the main putter head, allowing different putter head designs to be swapped without needing to remove or reinstall the shaft. Simply remove a few screws, install a new head, and you're ready to go. The shaft insert has a lie angle of 74 degrees and a static loft angle of 3 degrees to match the feel of many center-shafted putters. The design of the head of the putter has been carefully made to ensure that the center of mass is aligned with both the center of the face and the shaft when all weights are inserted. Therefore, the design of this putter naturally eliminates the majority of the torque produced when swinging. This can make it significantly easier to keep the face square at impact. To improve feel, the striking face is printed from TPU, providing a soft but responsive impact that closely resembles the insert faces found on many premium putters. Including the printed parts, added weights, screws, and epoxy, the total mass of the head of the putter is right around 320g. Features High-MOI perimeter-weighted design Center of Mass positioned to produce Low Torque when swinging Modular construction with interchangeable putter heads TPU face insert for a soft, responsive feel Removable shaft adapter secured with screws Designed for commonly available hardware and weights Inexpensive and creative alternative to traditional putters Hope you can have as much fun with this project as I did and get to give it a try out on course! For instructions, materials, and a list of parts to purchase/use, see the information below! Happy printing! Modular Design: Find other compatible putter heads here! Tempest Putter - Low-Torque / Modular / High MOI Striker Putter - A Center-Shafted Modular Putter Material Selection Body / Shaft Insert - PETG is recommended for outdoor use and to withstand higher temperatures while being relatively easy to print. Face Insert - TPU provides a soft yet confident feel when striking the ball. Assembly Be sure to read all the following steps before beginning assembly of your putter! The order in which some of these steps are taken is very important! Print all required components in your favorite colors. Be sure to print each component in its recommended material. Support removal. This step can be rather difficult due to the way the model must be printed, so my recommendation is to work from the outside inwards. I've used normal supports for the flat-bottomed sections to allow for each of the gaps for the weights to be cleared in a singular piece. Press the TPU face into the putter body. Secure it by using super glue or epoxy. Install the weights. All weights should sit flat within the head of the putter when installed correctly. See the image below for the proper layout of weights. A total of 30 individual 0.25oz weights are to be inserted, with 4 stacked near the face and 2 stacked in all other locations. While removing the film on the weights (making them stick) is recommended, it is not required for the putter to work great. Doing so may reduce noises heard when making contact with the ball slightly but will make it more difficult to remove the weights if interchanging putter heads. Install the bottom plate to the putter head at the 5 holes around the perimeter. Ensure that the side which features cutouts matching the position of the weights is facing the inserted weights. Use 5x M3 x 3/8" wood screws (link provided below for the ones used). Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Cut down the putter shaft to your desired length (I cut mine down to 36in for my height). For a great step-by-step process to complete this, check out this YouTube video: How to Shorten a Putter with a Steel Shaft . Install the grip to your putter shaft. I recommend completing this step before installing the shaft adapter and putter head as there is less time to work and straighten out the grip in comparison. For a great guide to doing this, check out this other YouTube tutorial: How to Install a Putter Grip (jump to 3:00 in the video). Bolt the shaft adapter/insert into the putter head after sliding the shaft adapter into place from the top. Using 3x M3 x 3/8" wood screws, secure the bottom plate, main body, and adapter together through the bottom in the three central holes. Then, complete the installation by using one more screw in the hole near the top of the putter towards the back. Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Epoxy the shaft into the adapter by applying epoxy to the shaft and sliding it in from the top. The epoxy which is suggested has a long working time which allows you to rotate the putter shaft so the the grip precisely lines up with its correct orientation. My recommendation for alignment of the grip is as follows: look down the shaft and line up the flat part of the grip with the line on top of the putter which is parallel to the direction of your stroke. Once aligned properly, wipe away any excess epoxy from the top of the putter. Let the putter sit overnight so that the epoxy can fully cure. Next step, rolling putts!
