model_name: Can I lick it? - Magnetic Elements - Small
description: - The times are over where only Iron, Cobalt, Nickel and alike were magnetic. - Did you ever wonder what Uranium taste like? Did you ever think that there should be more potassium on your shopping list? Do you feel a lack of nerdy gadgets in your lab or office? This model isn't here to answer that but tell you what elements you definitely shouldn't lick. I have created this model inspired by other models like the one by @Leander_C and shirts as a gift for a friend in the chemistry field. Since I prefer printing things with a use rather that plain decorations I added a little hole for 4x2 magnets in each Element. Functionality: This is the Mini model of my fridge magnet pse board. It is reduced in dimensions and has no element numbers due to the smaller size. This board provides you with exactly 118 magnets (or 122 magnets in the meme version) for fridges and whiteboards, each Element individually. So whenever some nutrients are not on your menu, just add them! There is also a bigger version with element numbers. There are two models available, each in two print profiles for with/without AMS: An accurate representation of the PSE A version with a few added fun elements: Ah - The Element of surprise Oh - The Element of disapointment Me - My element. Whatever floats your boat 🔑 - The Key element. We all know it's elementary Xx - A fully Customizable Elementblock to your choice on a spare plate Fun side quest for this model: Play with the letters, create words, sentences and things in impossible composition. Please feel free to upload the best sentences you can create out of the elements! There are also 12 slots for magnets in the back of the base plate. In total you will need 130 (134 in the meme version) magnets, 118 of which you can use as fridge and whiteboard magnets individually. Printing: The model uses six colors in total: Black, Blue, Red, Green, Yellow and White. There are two print profiles for each version, one with an AMS and one for people without. For the profile with no AMS: First load the base colors, then load the color for the writing (e.g. white) at the pause of the print profile. I printed the model with a 0.4 mm nozzle but a 0.2 mm nozzle would create much better details. If you print the custom element you need to adjust the writing on the block. Assembly: You should use a flat piece or magnet dispensers to push the magnets in. Your Thumbs will thank you. Start with the magnets on the base plate. Push them in firmly from the back. Make sure they all have the same orientation. For the elements you should have the magnets facing the opposite orientation to avoid them getting pulled to the wrong spots in the baseplate. I found it easiest to stick a few on a magnetic board and start pushing the elements onto the magnets. Again: Use some tool for less pain in the tips of your thumbs. You will need a bit of glue to keep the Color Indicators in place on the base. Please note that you shouldn'shouldn't put the elements in place and then try to move the model. If you do chaos ensues and you might form some instable or dangerous molecules on your floor. Jokes aside: the magnets will attract each other when you move the whole model. Disclaimer: I fully created this model which is meant as a joke. It does not mean you can safely lick neither the print nor any elements, not even the green ones. the model is not suitable for curved surfaces! Have fun!

Anyone who has tried letting kids paint a standard 3D printed model (made of PLA or PETG) with watercolours or tempera knows it’s a struggle – the paint slides off the plastic surface, runs, and doesn't cover well. Plaster casts made from these TPU molds are a complete game-changer. Plaster has the perfect absorbency, so colors stick flawlessly, dry instantly, and look incredibly vibrant. You only need to print these flexible molds once, and you can cast plaster dinosaurs for your kids every single weekend, over and over again. 💡 Why TPU 95A? These molds are designed specifically for printing with TPU 95A flexible filament. Thanks to the unique compliance of this material, you don't have to worry about complex mold-release draft angles during modeling. The model is designed with an optimal wall thickness of 1.5 mm , which provides the perfect balance: the mold keeps its geometry perfectly and doesn't bulge under the weight of liquid plaster, yet it remains flexible enough that you can incredibly easily peel it off the hardened cast like a banana skin. No getting stuck, no broken details. 🛠️ Recommended Print Settings: Material: TPU 95A (e.g., Bambu TPU). Wall Thickness / Perimeters: 3 walls (crucial for maintaining the mold's stability). Infill: 10%. Note: Print directly from the rear spool holder of your printer, do NOT use the AMS , as flexible materials tend to get tangled and stuck in it! For a perfectly smooth inner surface, make sure your TPU is well dried before printing. 🧪 Step-by-Step Casting Guide for Kids: Preparation: Place the clean and dry TPU mold on a flat, stable surface. Pro Trick for Zero Bubbles: Lightly spray the inside of the mold with a spray bottle filled with water and a single drop of regular dish soap. The soap acts as a wetting agent – it lowers surface tension, allowing the plaster to flow flawlessly into the smallest details without leaving air bubbles on the surface. Alternatively, you can use a release agent made of wax dissolved in alcohol. Mixing the Plaster: Mix standard white hobby plaster with water according to the package instructions. Make sure to mix the consistency a bit thinner (like runny pancake batter) – this is very important to ensure the plaster flows easily and without resistance into all the fine details and crevices of the dinosaur. Pouring: Carefully pour the plaster into the mold. It is recommended to leave about 2–3 mm from the top rim for easier handling. Once poured, gently tap the mold against the table a couple of times (vibration) to release any remaining trapped air bubbles to the surface. Releasing the Mold: Wait about 20 to 30 minutes. Once the plaster is solid and warm to the touch (due to the exothermic reaction), gently peel the TPU mold away by bending it. Thanks to the 1.5 mm thin wall, it will come off effortlessly. Creative Finale: Let the cast dry completely (ideally in the sun or on a radiator until it turns bright white and "rings" when tapped). Then, just give your kids brushes, tempera, or acrylic paints and let them create!

A minimalist hand-driven planetarium that turns the six classical planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn — at astronomically accurate relative speeds. 10 cm wide, 5 cm tall. A desk piece that models the solar system (as it was known in the 1700s!). Why only 6 planets? I came across a gear train for a planetarium that was designed by Scottish astronomer James Ferguson in the mid-1700s. At the time, Uranus and Neptune had not been discovered. His design used a single stacked gear to drive 6 planets, and I thought it was cool! In order to print it however, I had to include a dedicated connector gear for Jupiter-Saturn, as the teeth would have been too small to be printed. Description of the model can be found page 300 here . Parts Required Requires 7 ball bearings with these diameters: Sun = 12 mm Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars = 6 mm Jupiter, Saturn = 8 mm I included spheres for printing, but I think marbles or ball bearings would look much better. You can get all you need for approx €10 on ali express . I used a copper ball for Earth just to add distinction. The Man, The Myth: Bob Lazar & S4 The story of Bob Lazar is the cornerstone of modern UFO lore. In 1989, Lazar went public with claims that he was hired to reverse-engineer extraterrestrial technology at S4 , a hidden facility carved into the mountainside near Papoose Lake, just south of Area 51. According to Lazar, he worked on one of nine different discs—specifically the sleek, stainless-steel-looking "Sport Model." He described the craft as having no visible welds, bolts, or wires, powered by an anti-matter reactor that synthesized gravity waves. Current Status & United Nuclear: Today, Bob continues to operate United Nuclear Scientific Equipment and Supplies , a company that provides everything from high-voltage supplies to radioactive isotopes for enthusiasts and researchers. Despite decades of scrutiny, Bob has remained consistent in his story. The New Amazon Special: "S4: The Bob Lazar Story" (2026): If you haven't seen it yet, the new documentary "S4: The Bob Lazar Story" on Amazon Prime is a game-changer. Directed by Luigi Vendittelli, this special features the most realistic CGI recreations of S4 ever produced, showing the interior levels exactly as Bob described them. This 3D model is designed to be the perfect physical companion to that special—allowing you to hold the very tech shown on screen. If you want a more "industrial" look for the reactor components, SUNLU PLA Meta is my go-to for high toughness and clean detail. IMPORTANT! ONLY GLUE THE MOVING PARTS TO THE ASSIGNED PIECE. 5.Slide the body tube rack down to up into the gear on the arm. You may need a little force, but only a little. 6.Hammer/push the two thicker stage pins through the assembled stage and into the stage support. description: This Rubber Band Powered Helicopter is a simple, fully 3D-printed flying model with no tail boom, no gears, no electronics, and no extra hardware. Just two contra-rotating rotors and a rubber band between them—that is the whole idea. Wind the rotors, store energy in the band, and let go. The top and bottom rotors spin in opposite directions, canceling torque so the body stays stable without a tail rotor. Lift comes from the combined action of both rotors working together. The design is intentionally minimal. Print the parts, add one rubber band, and you are ready to fly. No screws, bearings, motors, or purchased kit parts are required. ------------ A rubber band runs directly between the upper and lower rotors. There are no gears—the band connects the two rotors and does all the work. When you wind the model, the band twists and stores elastic energy. On release, the band unwinds and drives both rotors at the same time—but in opposite directions. Because the rotors turn against each other, their reaction torques cancel out. That is why this helicopter does not need a tail boom or tail rotor. The contra-rotating setup does the job in a clean, compact way. Everything you need is printed in plastic except the rubber band. The fuselage holds the two rotors in alignment and gives you something to grip while winding. ------------- - A 3D printer and filament - One rubber band - One drop of glue That is it. No other parts to buy or hunt for. --------------------- I printed mine on a Bambu Lab A1 mini using PLA. Keep prints light where you can; less weight means better lift from the same rubber band. Use a drop of glue to secure the hook to the upper rotor from the top.

Kinetic Galton Board A kinetic Galton board that demonstrates the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution instead of the usual Gaussian you get from a classic bead-and-peg Galton board. It went semi-viral on Instagram (4M+ views), so I'm publishing the files here for anyone who wants to build one. Watch it run: https://www.instagram.com/p/DZauWk2SiXA/ How it works There are two chambers, left and right. The left chamber holds about 400 balls resting on a slider above a fast-spinning cylinder fitted with two fins. The fins agitate the balls and inject energy into the system. The balls collide with each other and with the chamber walls, behaving like gas particles in a box. At the top-right corner of the left chamber there is a small hole, roughly one ball wide. A ball only escapes (effuses) through this hole when it arrives with the right velocity. On the right side there are about 14 bins. The bin dividers are slightly shorter than the height of the escape hole, so a ball that effuses has to fall a small distance before reaching the tops of the bins. The physics is the interesting part: Because the hole is about the size of a single ball, a ball leaving it has essentially no vertical velocity at the moment of escape. So the time it takes to fall the small gap to the bins is the same for every ball . With d = v·t and t constant, the horizontal distance a ball travels (and therefore the bin it lands in) is proportional to its speed at the moment of effusion . Read the bin, and you've effectively measured how fast that ball was moving when it escaped. Do this for all ~400 balls, which have been colliding and exchanging energy like gas molecules, and the bins fill in to trace out the signature Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution . Printing There are two versions depending on what motor you have. Version for CIM (FRC) I built mine around an FRC CIM motor , just because I had some lying around. They're big and frankly overkill for this, but a lot of FRC people have them on hand. If that's you, open the Version for CIM folder and print the STL files there. Version for 775 For everyone else, the most common suitable motor is a 775 . They're cheap and easy to get almost anywhere. Open the Version for 775 folder and print the parts there. Both folders also include the raw STEP files if you want to modify anything. Cover The cover on mine is laser-cut acrylic . If you don't have a laser cutter, there's an STL so you can print it instead out of a transparent material, it just won't be as clear as acrylic. If you want to chase clarity, look up guides on printing crystal-clear PETG, though I didn't have much luck with it myself. Balls You need about 400–600 balls . They are 4 mm diameter , so do not substitute airsoft BBs, those don't work. To save you from duplicating a ball 400 times in your slicer, there's a 20×20 grid of them included. A few notes: Add a brim when printing the grid, otherwise the balls pop off the build plate. The sliced result should look like this: After printing you'll have a sheet with all the balls attached to it. Don't try to pull them off by hand , you'll tear the sheet and it becomes a miserable job getting the sheet off the balls. Instead, use pliers and twist each ball off the sheet. It's tedious, but it works. 400 balls took me about 20 minutes. Assembly and operation You will need 1x 775 motor, 2x M4x8 bolts, 4x M3x8 bolts Assembly is straightforward Place the balls into the device. Insert the slider. Shake the balls into the left chamber. Important: Use the slider to drop the balls onto the agitator while it is already spinning . If the balls surround a stationary agitator and you try to spin it up, it will stall the motor and the whole thing jams. That's it, spin it up and watch the distribution build.

This is a geared version of Buckminster Fuller’s iconic geometry demonstration. I fell into this Buckminster Fuller Jitterbug rabbit hole after seeing Keishiro Ueki's Jitterbug Mechanism . A few printing notes: Silk filaments look really cool, but I recommend not using them for the nut or connector. If you do, print a test part of the connector and nut first. Assembly: The assembly is pretty straightforward. To begin, create a ring of 4 triangles of alternating colors. Then attach an alternating-colored triangle to each of the open nodes. Finally, link them together. It's not difficult, but there are a lot of them. Tips: Make sure the parts are inline when the gear teeth are meshed. Hold the connector and not the triangle when locking the nut, or you may cause it to slip a gear tooth. I found my first attempt pretty good, although it had some things that bothered me, so i made a new and better one :) Improved from my first design: using truer hypocycloidal gears instead of cycloidal gears. added chamfers to reduce elephant footing and smoothing the parts for easier assembly . added external ridges for tighter lids and better grip. increased internal tolerances for better fluidity and lower friction. Better backdriveability also as a side effect made it much smaller without reducing strength and resistance . You probably don't need help for assembling cuz it's pretty simple, but for consistency, for assembly: the cycloids needs: -to fit the output shaft: have a 90° offset, so that the valleys of one matches the peaks of the other, and the holes are aligned -to fit the eccentric crank shaft, slightly shift them until it fits the crank shaft then put the whole thing in the outer cycloid then close it with both lids You can also assemble it by closing the outer cycloid with a lid, placing the output shaft in, then a cycloid, then the internal part of the eccentric shaft, then the other cycloid, then the external part of the shaft, and finish it off by closing with the other lid, but this requires some knowledge about cycloidal drives.

description: Overview This is a fully 3D printed wheel and chassis system for a trap powered car — a classic physics and engineering project. The design was built for a 4th grade science fair project to investigate how wheel size and tire material affect how far a trap-powered car travels. Three experiments were run per configuration (18 total runs), covering three wheel sizes and two tire materials. The winning combination — large 200mm wheels with TPU rubber tires — averaged 49.1 meters (161 feet) on a single spring release! The car is powered by a standard snap-style rat trap, which stores energy in its spring and releases it through a string wound around the rear drive axle. This design intentionally uses a rat trap rather than a mouse trap — the larger spring arm and stronger spring store significantly more energy, which is why the car travels so far. Build Levels — Start Simple, Go Further This design has three levels of complexity. Print only what you need. Level Plates What You Get 1 — Build the Car Plate 1 only A complete, working trap powered car with small wheels. Great standalone toy or first project. 2 — Wheel Size Experiment Plates 1 + 2 and/or 3 Swap in medium or large rear wheels and measure how far the car travels with each. One variable, easy to test, clear results. 3 — Tire Material Experiment All 4 plates Add TPU rubber tires and compare plastic wheels versus rubber tires. Requires a direct drive printer for TPU. The full science fair setup. Most people only need Plate 1. Print more plates if you want to experiment. How It Works The car converts stored spring energy into motion. When the trap arm releases, it pulls a string wound around the rear drive axle, spinning the wheels and launching the car forward. As the car moves, elastic potential energy from the spring converts to kinetic energy (motion). Wheel size and tire material both matter: Larger wheels cover more distance per rotation and roll over small surface irregularities more easily Rubber (TPU) tires grip the surface better, transferring more energy into forward motion instead of losing it to wheel slip Printed Parts Structural Parts — print in PLA or PETG Part Qty 3MF File Notes Body 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 One mounts to each end of the spring trap Arm 1 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 Extends the trap arm for more string travel Arm Cap 1 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 Secures the arm extension to the trap arm Axle 4 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 2 hubs per axle × front + rear axle (fits 1/4" bamboo dowel) Wheel Small (100mm) 4 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 2 front (fixed) + 2 rear (small config) Wheel Medium (150mm) 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 2 Print Plate 2 twice for a pair Wheel Large (200mm) 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 3 Print Plate 3 twice for a pair Everything is in one 3MF file with 4 plates. Plate 1 includes 4 small wheels: 2 for the front axle (always small) and 2 for the rear axle (small-wheel configuration). For medium or large rear wheels, print Plate 2 or Plate 3 twice — front small wheels are already on Plate 1. Tire Treads — print in TPU 95A Part Qty 3MF File Notes Tire Small 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 4 See tire plate note below Tire Medium 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 4 See tire plate note below Tire Large 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 4 See tire plate note below Tires are optional — the car works with plastic wheels only (we tested both!). TPU tires make a big difference though — see the results table below. Tire plate note: Plate 4 uses TPU 95A with supports enabled — filament and supports are already configured in the 3MF. All three tire sizes are arranged concentrically on the plate — the rings nest inside each other because the smaller tires fit through the center hole of the larger ones. To get a matching pair, print Plate 4 twice. To print only one size, delete the other two objects in Bambu Studio before slicing. Non-Printed Materials 1× Rat trap — Victor M205-9 Wide Plastic Pedal (recommended) or equivalent large rat trap. Use a rat trap, not a mouse trap — the stronger spring is essential for distance. 2× Bamboo dowel, 1/4" diameter, ~17.5" long (front axle + rear drive axle). 12" may also work. Dowels vary in straightness and diameter — pick the straightest ones, especially for the axles. If a dowel fits loosely, a small drop of glue holds it. If too tight, try another from the pack. Fishing line (monofilament) — light and strong 1 small metal staple Print Settings Structural Parts (PLA or PETG) Layer height: 0.2mm Walls: 3 Infill: 15% (gyroid or grid) Supports: None required Bed: Textured PEI plate PLA is recommended for most users — it's easier to print and more than strong enough for this application. PETG was used in the original build and also works great. TPU 95A Tires Layer height: 0.2mm Walls: 3 Infill: 15% Print speed: 30–40 mm/s (slow down for TPU reliability) Supports: Enabled (pre-configured in the 3MF for Plate 4) Direct drive extruder required — disable AMS/multi-material system for TPU Assembly Instructions Mount the trap to the body — slide the snap trap into the body's mounting slots Install axles — push bamboo dowels through the front and rear axle holders on the body Attach wheels — press wheels onto the ends of the rear axle Press-fit tires — stretch TPU tires over each wheel rim gradually, working around the rim evenly. Take your time — forcing one side too quickly can crack the wheel. Install arm extension — attach the printed arm to the trap's spring arm using the arm cap Attach string — tie one end of fishing line to the tip of the arm extension. Press a staple into the center of the rear axle and bend one prong out as a small hook. Tie a loop at the other end of the string and hook it onto the staple. When the trap arm releases, it pulls the string until the loop slips off the staple — this clean release is what launches the car. How to Launch Set the trap arm back (use caution — keep fingers clear of the snap mechanism) Wind the string around the center of the rear axle (consistent winding keeps the car straight) Place the car on a smooth, flat surface behind your start line Release the trap arm — the car launches! Tip: Wind the string at the axle center every time. Off-center winding causes the car to veer left or right, reducing distance. String length matters: when fully wound, the loop should slip off the staple just as the trap arm reaches its resting position. Too short and it releases before full energy is transferred; too long and the string tangles in the axle after release. Running It as an Experiment This design was built for a science fair, and it works great as a controlled experiment. Here's how to set one up: 1. State your hypothesis Make a prediction before you test. For example: "I think larger wheels will make the car go farther because each rotation covers more distance." 2. Identify your variables Independent variable (what you change): wheel size, or tire material Dependent variable (what you measure): distance traveled, or time rolling Constants (what stays the same): launch surface, string winding, number of winds, who releases the arm 3. Run multiple trials Do at least 3 runs per configuration and record each individually. Use the average — single runs vary too much to be reliable. 4. Record your data Wheel Size Tire Material Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 Average Small 100mm Plastic Small 100mm Rubber (TPU) Medium 150mm Plastic Medium 150mm Rubber (TPU) Large 200mm Plastic Large 200mm Rubber (TPU) 5. Analyze and conclude Compare your averages. Did the results match your hypothesis? What surprised you? Consider what other variables might have affected your results (surface texture, string length, dowel straightness). Notes & Tips The car can travel a surprisingly long distance — 49 meters is half a football field! Make sure you have plenty of room Surface quality matters — bumps, cracks, and slope all affect results Rubber bands can be used instead of TPU tires as a quick alternative for traction Front wheels are small fixed wheels and don't need to change between experiments Bamboo dowels vary from pack to pack — test a few and use the straightest ones. Axle fit affects both alignment and roll distance.

description: 这是一款机械日地月运行轨道仪，它通过精密的齿轮传动系统，生动模拟了太阳、地球与月球三者之间的运行轨迹和相对位置关系。 这款仪器不仅是一件精美的机械模型，更是一个直观的天文教学工具。它通过手摇曲柄驱动内部齿轮组，带动地球模型绕太阳公转，同时月球模型绕地球公转，完美再现了天体运行的基本规律。其核心设计在于通过不同齿数的齿轮组合，精确还原了地球公转与月球公转的周期比例，使演示过程既科学又富有观赏性。 仪器的中心是一个金色的太阳模型，周围环绕着标有“一月”至“十二月”的刻度盘，用于指示地球在公转轨道上的位置，从而帮助理解四季更替。月球模型则通过一个独立的臂架连接在地球模型上，随着地球一起绕太阳运动，同时自身也在绕地球旋转。 这类仪器的历史可以追溯到18世纪的“七政仪”（orrery），最初用于演示太阳系行星运动。现代版本的三球仪则更专注于日、地、月三者关系，广泛应用于中小学教学、科技馆展览以及天文爱好者收藏。它不仅能演示地球的自转与公转、月球的公转，还能形象地展示日食、月食、月相变化等天文现象，是理解基础天文学概念的绝佳辅助工具。

description: A Rattleback is a strange little physics toy that seems to break the rules: spin it one way and it spins normally, spin it the other way and it starts to wobble, stops, then reverses direction by itself. This model was designed around what matters most for a good 3D printed Rattleback: a strong self-reversing effect and easy printing with simple post-processing (no sanding required) Works Straight Off the Printer The print profile orients the model so the curved rattleback contact surface comes out smooth and functional without sanding. It does require supports, but removing them is much easier than sanding and tuning the underside until the effect works. Strong Self-Reversing Effect I tested and refined the rattleback shape by printing and comparing many different versions. After A LOT of testing, I found the perfect shape which can achieve up to around 3 full 360° spins in the “wrong” reverse direction ! It's probably not possible to make it perform much better, but, if you want to try, you can adjust the shape by using the “Customize” button to modify the parametric model, let me know if you find a better shape so I can update the default model! Best Surface for Maximum Effect The surface you spin the rattleback on matters a lot! To get the best reverse-spin effect, use a hard, smooth surface like glass, hard plastic or wood. Too much or too little friction can reduce the effect, or even stop it from working. A dusty surface can ruin the effect too! It’s a small print, but it makes a great physics demo, desk toy or “magic trick” to show friends.

model_name: My Social Battery — “how charged do I feel?”
description: My Social Battery — a tactile “how charged do I feel?” slider for kids Slide the lightning bolt and click through five stages — from flat-battery exhausted to fully charged — to show, at a glance, how much social/emotional energy you’ve got left. It’s a friendly, fidget-satisfying self-regulation and communication aid shaped like an AA battery. Built for kids 4–11 , and great for SEND / AAC / visual-support classrooms and calm corners — but honestly it’s for anyone who’s ever run out of “people battery.” Why you’ll like it A proper click. A print-tuned ratchet gives a crisp tick between stages and a firmer “settle” at each of the five homes — and it clicks exactly the same force in both directions (a symmetric twin-arm spring, not a one-sided one). Chunky lightning-bolt handle — rounded and wide, sized to survive a five-year-old, easy for little fingers to grab. Five emoji faces on removable colour panels: 😵 exhausted → 🙁 low → 😐 okay → 🙂 good → 😀 fully charged. Swap the panels toollessly — they snap in and pop out, so you can re-theme it (a 6-panel feelings set is on the way). Wall-mount or hand-hold — two rear keyholes or a Command-Strip on the flat back. Print settings Material: PLA. Stiff/standard PLA gives the crispest click (the spring is tuned for it). Nozzle / layers: 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layers. ~15 % infill is plenty. Supports: Tree supports for the Body only (they release much more cleanly than normal supports). Everything else prints support-free. Orientation (as exported): Part Orientation Supports Body front face up tree supports (for the channel roof / pockets) Slider flat (as exported) none — the spring must print flat so it flexes in-plane Grip (bolt) flat, bolt-face on the bed none Back cover flat none Panels ×5 flat none Two-colour panels: print each panel in its stage colour and swap to black at the face layer (Z ≈ 2.0 mm) so the embossed emoji prints black. On an AMS this is automatic; otherwise it’s a single manual filament change. Colours (suggested): Panel 1 red · 2 orange · 3 yellow · 4 light green · 5 dark green; body white/grey; bolt gold/yellow. Assembly (a couple of minutes, one drop of glue) The grip is a separate part because it’s far too wide to thread through the front slot. Drop the Slider into the body channel from the back — the square post pokes out through the front slot. From the front, press the Grip onto the post ( a drop of super-glue = a permanent, kid-proof bond). Press the Back cover into its rebate from behind until the sprung tabs snap home (firm tug to service later). Snap the five Panels into the front pockets (pop them out later via the sloped pry-notch at the bottom edge). Mount: two rear keyholes (slide onto screws) or a Command-Strip on the flat back. Notes Wall-mount screws: the keyholes suit M3.5 screws — pop the screws into the wall first and slide the plaque down. Little parts: there are no loose small parts once assembled (the grip is glued; panels are captive snap-fits).

model_name: SMARS rover remake for use with ESP32-WROVER-CAM
description: I've printed the SMARS tracked rover to see if I can adapt to use an ESP32-WROVER-CAM Dev.B microcontroller which has a built-in 2Mpx camera so I can turn it into a tracked mobile, WiFi controlled webcam. Although the ESP32-WROVER-CAM has enough GPIOs to use with the L298N dual motor driver, when the webcam is turned on in the sketch along with the WiFi, there are only 4 usable GPIOs remaining. Luckily, I found that it should be possible to use just the 4 GPIOs to control the two motors, but it also requires that the L298N EN-A and EN-B pins be raised to +5V. If you discarded the two jumpers that usually come with the L298N, then use two DuPont wires to connect the two enable pins on the driver to +5V. The print profile available for the BambuLab A1 Mini worked perfectly although I cannot use the IR sensor mount since the chassis is fully occupied by the L298N and the 2S1P 18650 pack with switch and voltmeter, but more importantly, there are no more GPIOs left to use the IR sensor. As you can see from the photo I took of the result is not very good looking but it does move quite nicely. I have two 100rpm DC motors which give it a decent scurry speed. The code I can share upon request if anyone wants to give it a go. Ping me and I can share the sketch and describe the wiring since it took a bit of experimenting to get the ESP32 to eventually be able to control the two motors as desired.

model_name: Spin & Solve – A Modular Educational Math Toy
description: Spin & Solve transforms everyday math practice into a playful experience where children learn by touching, spinning, writing, and solving. By combining simple mechanical interaction with educational value, the toy encourages curiosity, independent thinking, and joyful learning. Spin & Solve is a modular educational toy designed to make mathematics playful, engaging, and interactive for young children. The toy consists of three rotating blocks: two number blocks and one operator block. Children spin each block to generate random mathematical equations and then solve them independently. The first number block generates a random number, the center block selects a mathematical operator, and the second number block generates another number. The child then writes the equation in a notebook and solves it, transforming traditional math practice into an enjoyable game. The design encourages children to learn through hands-on interaction. The rotating arrows provide satisfying motion, while the colorful elements capture attention and maintain engagement. Since every combination is random, children can create hundreds of unique equations, making learning both challenging and fun. The toy is designed as a multipart 3D print, allowing it to be manufactured on any standard single-color 3D printer without requiring expensive multicolor printing systems. Individual components can be printed separately and assembled easily, making the design accessible, customizable, and sustainable. Key Features Interactive spinning mechanism Random equation generation Encourages self-learning and problem-solving Improves number recognition and arithmetic skills Develops handwriting through written exercises Bright, child-friendly colors Safe rounded edges and simple operation Modular and easy-to-assemble design Compatible with standard single-color 3D printers Educational Benefits Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division practice Fine motor skill development Independent learning Logical thinking and problem-solving Increased engagement through play

Capture Incredible Timelapses With The AllSky Capsule. The AllSky Capsule is a camera system for astrophotography. It constantly records images of the sky, both night and day, and compiles timelapses using the captured images. I have developed the AllSky Capsule to use Aaron Morris' indi-allsky software. https://github.com/aaronwmorris/indi-allsky There are many other AllSky software packages available, and I have designed another Allsky Enclosure in the past using Thomas Jacquin's AllSky . This version, The AllSky Capsule, is inspired by the Ikea BEGÅVNING Glass Dome . Costing just £13, I couldn't resist the opportunity to try and fit an AllSky system inside. The AllSky Capsule is built around Arducam's LN051 120 Degree Ultra Wide Angle Lens . I Have chosen this lens for several reasons. Firstly, the cost is very good for the quality of the optics; secondly, the image it produces is almost perfectly flat. I didn't want any distortion or fish-eyeing, it is the largest FOV I could find without significant distortion. Lastly, it seems to be widely available. Much like the Ikea Dome, it should be easy for everyone to acquire. Indi-allsky supports a large range of sensors and modules. I have included a BME680 environmental sensor, a TSL2591 light sensor, and a GPS module. A Raspberry Pi 5, with a Waveshare PoE HAT+ (C), Active Cooler, and 256gb M.2 SSD hosts the indi-allsky install. There is also a System Fan to help keep things cool. Features. A simple educational electromagnetic motor powered by a battery, copper coil, and magnet. Perfect for learning the basics of electricity, magnetism, and motor mechanics. Designed as an easy beginner electronics project with a clean 3D printed base. How to Build: This simple electromagnetic motor works by using a battery, a copper wire coil, and a permanent magnet to create rotational movement. First, bend two paper clips so they can hold the coil while still allowing it to spin freely. Attach the paper clips to the battery or the 3D-printed holder using electrical tape, making sure they are stable and properly aligned. Next, create a coil by winding insulated copper wire into a circular shape with around 6–10 turns, leaving two wire ends sticking out on each side. Carefully remove the insulation from the wire ends: only strip the insolation from one site this is impotent if done on both it wont function. This allows the electric current to switch on and off during rotation, which keeps the motor spinning. Place the coil into the paper clip supports so it can rotate with minimal friction. Then position a permanent magnet directly underneath the coil. Once the battery is connected, give the coil a small push with your finger. The magnetic field generated by the current inside the coil interacts with the permanent magnet, causing the coil to continuously rotate and creating a simple electric motor. 晨昏线与南极圈相切，南极圈内极昼，北极圈内极夜。 6.3 春分、秋分无极昼极夜 公转至春分或秋分刻度，太阳直射赤道，晨昏线过两极，全球昼夜等长，无极昼极夜。 6.4 极昼极夜范围渐变演示 缓慢连续转动公转主臂，观察极昼/极夜范围从极点逐步扩大至极圈，再逐步缩小的动态过程，完整还原全年变化。 7. 月相、日食、月食完整演示（结合黄白交角） 7.1 月相周期演示 开启光源，手动转动 月球公转轴 ，月球沿白道面公转。观察月球被照亮部分的形状变化： 新月（朔）→娥眉月→上弦月→盈凸月→满月（望）→亏凸月→下弦月→残月→新月。 （因潮汐锁定，月球同一面始终朝向地球，但被照亮区域随公转位置变化。） 7.2 日食演示（朔日限定） 将月球转至 日—地之间（朔点） ，并微调月球公转角度以抵消黄白交角偏差，使日、月、地三者近似共线。此时月球影子落在地球上，可演示日全食/日偏食效果。 解释 ：因黄白交角存在，多数朔日不共线，故日食罕见。 7.3 月食演示（望日限定） 将月球转至 日—地延长线（望点） ，微调角度使日、地、月共线，地球阴影覆盖月球，演示月食。同理，并非每望日都发生。 8. 标准操作注意事项 四轴结构精密，转动需轻柔匀速，禁止暴力操作。 常规演示中地轴岁差旋进轴应保持锁定 ，仅当演示岁差或初始校准时方可调节。 演示晨昏线、极昼极夜、日月食时，建议在暗光环境下进行。 可根据需要自主适配光源亮度与供电方式。 设备为精密模型，禁止摔落、撞击、浸泡；儿童操作需成人陪同。 禁止私自拆卸轴体，以免四轴联动精度失效。 9. 常见故障与原理答疑 Q1：为什么月球不会自转？是否为缺陷？ A：不是缺陷。真实月球为潮汐锁定，自转与公转周期相同，永远同一面朝地。本设备科学还原该特性。 Q2：为什么演示四季时不需要转动地轴岁差旋进旋钮？ A：真实地球公转中，地轴在空间中的指向保持恒定（指向北极星附近）。四季更替完全由公转位置改变太阳直射点而产生。若在公转中手动旋转地轴，将得到错误原理。本设备的地轴岁差旋进轴仅用于初始校准或演示岁差。 Q3：为什么太阳模型比地球小？ A：这是为了桌面教学的可行性而进行的工程缩放。真实比例无法在桌面模型中实现，本设备牺牲尺寸比例但保留了所有角度、光照几何和相对运动关系，不影响任何天文现象的教学。 Q4：黄白交角5°09′是如何实现的？月球没有自转轴会影响吗？ A：黄白交角是月球公转轨道面（白道面）与地球公转轨道面（黄道面）的夹角，通过倾斜的月球公转副臂机械实现，与月球是否自转无关。本设备正确保留该夹角，用于演示日月食发生条件。 Q5：为什么无法每次朔望日都演示日月食？ A：设备精准还原了5°09′黄白交角，多数朔望日三者不共线，与现实一致，非故障。 Q6：极昼极夜、晨昏线演示效果不明显怎么办？ A：检查公转位置是否准确对应节气刻度，并确认地轴指向已锁定且倾角无误（未误触岁差旋钮）。重新按第4章归位即可。 Q7：晨昏线为什么不会和经线完全重合？ A：仅春分、秋分两天太阳直射赤道，晨昏线与经线重合；其余时间因地轴倾角，晨昏线与经线存在夹角，本设备可完整呈现该变化。

description: A steel transmission tower modeled on a real 765 kV lattice tangent tower design. Print details Footprint: 189 × 86 mm · Height: 247 mm Single piece, printed vertically Tree supports recommended A separate support-interface material is highly recommended. The lattice is dense and the members are fine — printing the interface layer in a non-bonding filament (e.g. PETG against a PLA part, or a dedicated support filament) makes the difference between supports that peel off cleanly and supports that fuse into the structure and ruin it. description: This mechanical gripper was developed as a Mechatronics Engineering thesis project to offer an economical, adaptable, and functional solution for academic environments. It utilizes a 4-bar mechanism (optimized to comply with Grashof's Law). It features flexible TPU 85A fingers based on the biomimetic "Fin Ray" principle. !!!!! Hinweis bitte vor dem Drucken die kompette Beschreibeung lesen !!!!! Dieses Getriebe ist Teil eines Projektes aus der Vorlesung Konstruktionslehre IV aus unserem Studium. Ich habe das Getriebe zusammen mit @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas und zwei anderen Kollegen entwickelt. Wir haben dies zusätzlich zu der Ausarbeitung abgegeben und sind mächtig stolz darauf. Es ist ein wunderbares Anschauungsmodell, welches weiter optimiert wurde als die ursprüngliche abgegebene Version. Hier die wichtigsten Infos zum Getriebe: - das Planetengetriebe ist Teil eines Antriebstranges einer Presse. Um das Getriebe herum befindet sich noch ein deutlich größeres Schwungrad, sowie eine Kupplung. - ich habe das Getriebe komplett aus PLA gedruckt, wie es sich mit anderen Materialien verhält weiß ich nicht - ich habe einen P1S von Bambulab und sehr feine Einstellungen gewählt. Ob das notwendig ist, weiß ich nicht. Das Ergebnis lässt sich aber auf jeden Fall sehen - ich würde das Getriebe nicht skalieren, da sich sonst Abstände zwischen Lager und Welle proportional erhöhen, diese jedoch aufeinander abgestimmt sind - Für ein komplettes Getriebe muss man die Platten 1-3 und 4 oder 5 drucken. Die Platte 4 enthält einen Ständer mit Fläche für ein Schild (Siehe in der pdf), die Platte 5 ein Ständer ohne Fläche für ein Schild. - nach meiner Farbkodierung ist: weiß die Antriebswelle, schwarz der Abtrieb von Planetenträger, grau das Gehäuse, rot die Zahnräder, grün die Lager und gelb der Stopfen bzw. die Schrauben - ich habe folgendes geklebt: die Stifte in das Gehäuse, den Stopfen in das Gehäuse, die inneren Lager, direkt am Gehäuse - die Deckel können auf das Gehäuse geklebt werden, dann kann das Getriebe jedoch nicht mehr auseinandergenommen werden. Damit das Getriebe trotzdem zusammenhält ist die Klammer da. Diese kann von unten auf das komplette Gehäuse geschoben werden - die Kleinen Lager gehen lassen sich nur sehr schwer in die Zahnräder pressen. Dafür diese vorsichtig mit etwas diese in die Zahnräder schlagen, bis die Lager deutlich unter der Kante des Zahnrades sind - der Deckel vom Planetenträger hat extra eine Aussparung, sodass man ein Zahnrad sieht. Die „Schrauben“, welche Wirklichkeit nur Stifte sind, gingen bei mir sehr schwer. Wenn ihr das Getriebe wieder gut aufmachen können wollt, diese am besten ein wenig kleiner Skalieren und evtl. an den Deckel vom Planetenträger kleben - das angehängte pdf enthält die Beschriftung (52mmx22mm), ich habe dies auf Papier (DIN A4) ausgedruckt, welches man als Aufkleber verwenden kann. Es lässt sich aber auch mit normalem Papier ausdrucken und aufkleben - das ganze Getriebe mit Gestell braucht ca. 130g Filament - ich habe für die Stützen unter dem Gehäuse ein paar Schichten Support for PLA verwendet. Wenn kein Support for PLA Filament vorhanden ist dies einfach zu PETG ändern. Das funktioniert genauso. (Wenn das Getriebe aus PETG gedruckt wird dann zu PLA wechseln) Daher kommen auch ein paar wenige Filamentwechsel. Wer dies möchte einfach das Profil normale Stützen drucken. Ich habe insgesamt 5 Modelle gedruckt bis das Getriebe die finale Version hattte. Viel Spaß damit! english version: This gearbox is part of a project from the “Design Engineering IV” course in our degree program. I developed the gear together with @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas and two other colleagues. We submitted this in addition to our term paper and are incredibly proud of it. It’s a wonderful demonstration model that has been further optimized beyond the original version we submitted. Here’s the key information about the gearbox: - The planetary gearbox is part of a press’s drive train. Surrounding the gearbox is a significantly larger flywheel, as well as a clutch. - I printed the gearbox entirely out of PLA; I don’t know how it would behave with other materials. - I used a Bambulab P1S and selected very fine settings. I’m not sure if that was necessary. In any case, the result is definitely impressive. - I wouldn’t scale the gearbox, as doing so would proportionally increase the distances between the bearings and the shaft, which are designed to be precisely matched. - To build a complete gearbox, you need to print plates 1–3 and either 4 or 5. Plate 4 includes a support with space for a label (see the PDF); plate 5 includes a support without space for a label. - According to my color coding: white is the drive shaft, black is the output shaft of the planetary carrier, gray is the housing, red is the gears, green is the bearings, and yellow is the plugs or screws - I glued the following parts in place: the pins into the housing, the plug into the housing, and the inner bearings directly to the housing - The covers can be glued to the housing, but then the gearbox can no longer be taken apart. The clip is there to keep the gearbox together anyway. It can be slid onto the entire housing from below - The small bearings are very difficult to press into the gears. To do this, gently tap them into the gears with a small tool until the bearings are clearly below the edge of the gear. - The cover of the planetary carrier has a special cutout so you can see a gear. The “screws”—which are actually just pins—were very difficult for me to insert. If you want to be able to open the gearbox easily again, it’s best to scale these down slightly and possibly glue them to the cover of the planetary carrier - The attached PDF contains the label (52mm x 22mm); I printed this on paper (DIN A4), which can be used as a sticker. However, you can also print them on regular paper and stick them on. - The entire gearbox with the frame requires about 130g of filament. - I used the Super Cool Track Pro plate for the housing and the Textured PEI Plate for the rest. That’s how it’s set up. If you use different plates, be sure to take this into account! - I used a few layers of “Support for PLA” for the supports under the housing. If you don't have “Support for PLA” filament, simply switch to PETG. It works just the same. (If the gearbox is printed in PETG, switch to PLA.) That's why there are a few filament changes. If you don't want those, just change the support settings in the slicer back to normal supports. I printed a total of 5 models before the gearbox reached its final version. Have fun with it!

tags: drawbridge gate|medieval gate|medieval door|dnd interactive|dnd|pulley|dnd functional|mechanism|pulley mechanism
description: To be honest, I've only played D&D a handful of times. The first time, I joined a campaign that was already in progress, and my character's role ended up being... a loot box (a very important role for the story, of course!). The second time was playing Baldur's Gate 3 on the highest difficulty. We made it all the way to level 4... and then we lost :( Since this contest is all about imagination and role playing, I wanted to create something that felt interactive instead of just decorative. I started looking for drawbridge models, and to my surprise, there weren't many available (especially ones inspired by D&D) so I decided to design one myself. The mechanism is actually quite simple. It uses three pulleys and a hand crank to raise and lower the bridge. Surprisingly, the most challenging was decorating the model and making it look like a proper medieval gate (i mean, i tried). This is both the largest and longest print I've ever made, using close to 500 grams of filament. I tried to reduce material usage as much as possible, especially in the base, which prints with just 5% infill. Thankfully, all of the print plates completed without any issues. The model is optimized to print without an AMS. If you'd like a two color gate/door, you can simply add pause commands during the print to swap filament. For the finishing touches, I added small grilles, and a couple of crocodiles in the water. I also took the opportunity to try some plastic safety eyes I bought on AliExpress, and they really add a lot to the final result. That said, I've also included printable eyes if you prefer a fully printed build. I'm going to try to upload an assembly video (video only, no audio). The assembly process is very straightforward, but I think it could still be helpful. If you're interested in printing the model and have any questions, feel free to ask! Materials ~20 cm of yarn/wool , Used as the rope for the pulley system. I experimented with shoelaces, but they didn't provide enough friction. Glue , For final assembly. A tool for support removal , Most parts print support-free, but the door/gate itself requires a few supports that can be a bit difficult to remove. If possible, printing the supports in PETG can make removal much easier.

Polyhedra Generator – All 31 Platonic, Archimedean & Catalan Solids (Solid or Wireframe) One parametric model, 31 classic polyhedra : the 5 Platonic solids, all 13 Archimedean solids, and all 13 Catalan solids — each printable as a full solid or as an elegant wireframe made of round struts along the edges. Pick a solid, set the edge length, choose solid or wireframe, hit Generate. That's it. ✨ Features 31 solids in one file — from the humble tetrahedron to the 180-strut disdyakis triacontahedron True mathematical geometry — exact canonical coordinates; Catalan solids are derived at render time as duals of their Archimedean counterparts via polar reciprocation Solid or wireframe mode — display piece or airy lattice Print-ready options — strut diameter, reinforced vertex nodes, and an automatic flat base cut for reliable first layers Size echo — the console reports vertices, edges, actual edge lengths and the circumscribed diameter, so you know the real footprint before slicing 🔧 Parameters Parameter What it does solid Which of the 31 polyhedra to generate edge_length Edge length in mm (for Catalans: the longest edge) mode solid or wireframe strut_size Strut diameter (wireframe) — keep ≥ 2.5–3 mm for FDM node_size Optional larger spheres at the vertices to reinforce joints base_cut Trims a thin slice off the bottom for a flat, stable bed contact rotation Lay a face flat on the plate (solids generate in canonical orientation) 🖨️ Printing tips Wireframes up to ~50 mm edge length print without supports in most cases: struts of 3 mm, 100% cooling, slow outer walls Larger wireframes: enable tree supports for the near-horizontal top struts Keep base_cut at 0.4 mm — it turns a tangent contact point into a proper flat patch Handling it a lot? Set node_size ~1 mm above strut_size Solid mode: use rotation or your slicer's lay flat on face , and 5–10% infill The print profile contains only the solid cube and the wireframe, as including all 62 solids would have been cumbersome and of little use. INFO These are magnetic separation racks for 0.2mL PCR sized tubes. Works for SPRI, ConA, or any magnetic beads. My lab is a big fan of the epicypher racks but they cost $500 dollars so we were always fighting over the one, and even then when you have more than 8 or 16 samples it is inconvenient to always switch out tubes while doing high through put experiments. I wanted more racks so I designed these with a similar style and functionality to the epicypher racks with some added improvements. 1.Racks come in 8-tube and 12-tube sizes so you can make full use of the multichannel and scale up easier 2.Magnets are removable, so you can simply slide the magnet out rather than removing the tubes from the rack 3.The magnet can be turned around to work better for either small or large volumes. 4. Less than 1% of the price of Epicypher magnet racks (even with the cost of magnets) BEFORE YOU PRINT While smooth, semi-textured, and textured plates all work, I find that printing on a textured plate results in a tighter fit of the magnet holders inside the rack. I prefer the slightly looser fit I get when printing on my BIQU cool plate. If you use my print profile then you don't need any supports, however, these are kind of tall prints so I recommend making sure you have a clean bed and dried filament to avoid any adhesion errors. If you are having adhesion problems then you can take it a step farther and use a cool plate and/or a brim. ASSEMBLY You will need 10x5x3mm magnets. One 8 tube rack takes 16 magnets and one 12 tube rack takes 24 magnets. After printing, glue the two halves of the magnet holder together with the magnet holes in the same orientation. Then, insert the magnets. While they have a snug press fit, I find that they stay in better if the magnets on either side of the holder have opposite poles facing each other (the orientation where they stick together). A dab of super glue doesn't hurt either.

I remixed this model to improve the teeth a little and make them easier to glue in. The six front teeth roots may need to be sanded down a little for best fit, or just reduce the size of them a tiny bit in the slicer so they fit all the way into the tooth sockets. Because the back molars have more complicated roots, they will not just slip back into the sockets like the front ones do. For those I cut off the roots and added small posts to allow for better gluing. There are two sets of back molars for each side. One set is for placing as a full set of teeth, the others are for placing as single teeth for a more gap-toothed look. Use whichever you prefer. I recommend painting the teeth and skull separately, then coat the teeth in clear epoxy before gluing them into the skull. Take care to keep careful track of the teeth positions because it is easy to mix them up. You can stick them to a piece of tape to keep them in order.

description: I was printing Marimo Labs' excellent Water Rocket Launcher , which involves feet with printable stakes for anchoring the system. My planned launchpad area was on concrete, which doesn't work well with printable stakes, so I decided to redesign the bottom of the leg to reduce the size of the stake hole to support mounting to a heavier wood base with a screw and washer. I used a heavy piece of 1.5" thick painted particle board, which adds enough weight that you can insert the pin easily. It also makes putting the launcher at an angle much safer, if you are going for distance or competing with the wind. Later we took the setup to a large park, and the launcher was instantly set up and secured with the added weight of the base. The print profile includes a plate that uses a modifier part to increase the infill around the mounting hole. I printed one without this reinforcement and it worked perfectly, but for an extra 3 minutes and less than a gram of filament, you get a little extra insurance against over tightening your screw and crushing the walls of the print. This is by far the best launching system I have seen, and it was quick and efficient to print. Highly recommended. With these updated feet mounted to a heavy base, setup is quick and easy, regardless of location.

This high-efficiency mousetrap car is powered purely by the spring mechanical energy of a Windhager mousetrap and utilizes a real gear system to maximize distance. The design runs incredibly smooth and achieved a personal track record of exactly 30 meters! To wind it up, the car must be rotated by three-quarters of a turn at the main gear, featuring a gear ratio of 1 to 64. Required Hardware: 6x 6700 ZZ Ball Bearings (10 x 15 x 4 ) 1x M3 Socket Head Screw 43 mm total length, partially threaded with a 20 mm smooth shank 1x Windhager Mousetrap Step-by-Step Guide: Spring Preparation: Remove the spring from the Windhager mousetrap. Trim the protruding wire ends so that about 2 cm remain, and bend them so they stick out at a 90° angle relative to the spring. Inserting the Spring & Sleeve: Push the printed plastic sleeve inside the spring. Then, insert the spring into the main motor cavity of the chassis with the thicker side of the spring facing inward. Main Gear & Core Screw: Place the large main drive gear onto the spring. Pass the M3 screw through the gear and the spring to lock everything into place. Tighten it enough to eliminate wobbling, but ensure it remains loose enough to spin freely without excessive friction. Gearbox Assembly: Press one ball bearing into each of the middle gears. If the fit is tight, gently tap them in using a hammer. Carefully mount these geared assemblies onto their designated pins on the chassis. Axles & Wheel Bearings: Install the axles along with the remaining bearings onto the frame. Tip: For the wheel axles, you can optionally use 3D-printed bearings. However, for the high-load drivetrain gears (Step 4), real metal ball bearings are strictly required! Attaching the Wheels: Finally, press-fit the wheels onto the axles – the large wheels go in the back, and the small wheels go in the front.

I wanted to electroplate my models and investigated online for suiting models. Found none that I was happy with. So I decided to design and build my own. The design consists of three main parts: 1) the motor assembly 2) the controlbox 3) the arc bridge assembly The motor assembly is designed so it can easily be fitted on different sized arc bridges, because not all containers have the same width/height requirements. I will share the dimensions of the current container i used, orderable off amazon. If you have another container, I will share the SCAD file as well, so you can easily adapt the width to your needs. Keep in mind that the min dia is always the width of the motormount plate and standoffs to the side of the container. The motor assembly itself houses the stepper (28BYJ-48) and the ULN2003 motor driver board. The controlbox has a couple of easy to acquire and solder components: an ESP32 board (i used a SEED XIAO ESP32-C6, very small board), a LM2596 buck converter, a rotary encoder (KY-040) to control the speed, a battery and an on/off switch. I will share the scheme here as well. The ESP firmware will also be shared (rename the main.c.txt to main.c) IMPORTANT NOTE; make sure to trim your buck convertor to 5v before connecting anything to it, otherwise it may be set too high and you will fry your electronics The arc bridge is pretty straightforward; it clamps on to the side of the container (dont overdo it, just keeps it from moving around) and comes with a nut to secure the motor assembly in place. I also designed a model hook that allows a straight copper wire down into the bath, by easily sticking the wire in from below, where it exits on the side and you can loop it around the rough thread of the hook. this is a 10/10 connection to your model. Moreover; this allows you to prep and test your hookup before you connect it to the hook of the rotary and allows for multiple models to be prepared in parallel. In functional terms; the device is powered either through usb or through a 9v block in the compartment of the control box, it's wired to prefer the USB power when available. The movement is started by pushing in the rotary encoder button, that controls start/stop movement. then turning the knob controls the speed of movement. The movement is designed as an oscillator; it turns 1,25 times and then reverses that movement. This is to make sure your connecting wire (to the negative lead) doesnt get looped (ruining your electrical connection). I added the whole setup in one .3mf on two plates. enjoy and let me know if you have questions or are happy with your build !

A simple gear set I created for a maker day event at the library. I would have preferred to just use something that was already out there, but as is typical for me, I began to want certain features / tweaks, so I just made my own. These were modeled in TinkerCAD using the gear generator shape. I wanted: something small and simple and lite for kids a grid / board that supports a large number of combinations of gear connections a way to drive the gears without turning them by hand an indicator for direction they were turning Ended up with: 5mm spaced grid board Works with 10T, 12T, 18T, 20T, 21T, 24T, 30T, 31T, 40T gears (most perfectly, some combinations have a tiny spacing error) Small hole direction indicator Handle / driver PDF activity for kids (8+) I initially didn't want to use pegs and fully open pegboard holes because I wanted the gears to be standard with hole in the center and no attached peg. So I initially started with a true board of pegs for gears to slip onto, but then realized I would be very limited with gear placement without some deep hubs on the gears to clear the peg heights. So then I moved onto a design with gears that slotted onto removeable pegs with separate c-clips to keep them on (like @osamutake models). The pegs screwed into slots on the board and then c-clips locked the gears onto them. This worked, but then I realized it wasn't so simple for kids, and the print resolution would have to be very fine to ensure threads were clean and c-clips were strong enough for kids to not break them. Kids screwing pegs in and out of the board and snapping c-clips into place, especially if the prints weren't perfectly clean, was going to be a problem.. So finally I reluctantly accepted a pluggable gears design into a holed pegboard as posted (similar to design by @Ioannis Tsar). The grid spacing evolved from 10mm to 5mm to support more gears. Also evolved from a hexagonal shape to conserve space and keep diagonal distances equilateral, but then the 5mm hypotenuses worked even with small spacing errors, so kept the grid shape for simplicity. The handle didn't work great and could be redesigned. This was my 3rd design, but still not driving the gears as well as hoped. Could definitely benefit from redesign. I had to print about 100 pieces of everything (sans 40T gears), so needed fast prints. Profile defaults to Random seam so seam is less of a hurdle. A grid bound at 0% sparse infill, draft 0.24mm layer print worked fine for me for my event. Gears were printed with 10% infill. A few posts snapped if kids were rough, so consider higher infill for longer lasting model. Sanding posts definitely helps but is time consuming. I would only recommend if you wanted to keep the kit around for a long time. If it's a one-off event, the gears work fine once snapped in and turned a bit.

This is my Astronomy Without Borders Onesky 130F5 upper tube assembly. I found two major deficiencies with the original upper tube assembly. The sloppy threads in the helical focuser, that does not have adequate rigidity The finicky secondary mirror collimation The sloppy threads in the original helical focuser is well known with kludgy fixes like wrapping the threads in Teflon tape or using grease on the threads… But the bigger problem was the thin plastic cantilevered design. If you tried using any moderately heavy eyepieces the weight was cause it to sag and vibrate intolerably at higher magnifications, making planetary observing incredibly frustrating. And for some reason that I can not imagine, people making these entry level telescopes put the spring between the secondary mirror and the hub thingy. When you loosen the locking screw the whole thing just goes wherever it wants and makes collimation a total pain. Also, having the whole assembly on the one round rod made one more axis it could rotate on and need adjusting. Very annoying. In this upper tube assembly, the whole things is printed thick and solid, allowing for the mounting of a full size Crayford focuser. This upper assembly is very solid and has very little deflection. It uses a four vane spider, and I relocated the spring to the top side of the hub so it's in a push/pull orientation. Now when you loosen the center screw a turn or two, the spring holds the mirror mount against the three screws so you can actually see what effect your adjustments have on your collimation. As an added benefit, the holes for the strut rods are much deeper, which leaves a lot less unsupported rod length further increasing stiffness. And finally, I rotated the focuser around a bit for easier seated observing. IMO, the stock orientation seemed better for standing and hunching over the telescope. Now the focuser is at a 45° angle which I think offers better ergonomics. There are a couple of compromises though. First, it makes the telescope very top heavy. I had to slide the dovetail all the way as far as it can go, and it's still not 100% perfectly balanced but it's good enough. And second, the large Crayford sticks out axially further than the original focuser, requiring the use of 22mm spacers limiting how far the telescope extends to achieve focus. This is the focuser: https://agenaastro.com/gso-crayford-focuser-reflector-telescope-dual-speed-eaf-1-25.html Use the 176mm base curvature option. The design also utilizes this dovetail mounting shoe https://a.co/d/0iBxRjiH It is designed for m6 screws but I wanted to only use M4 on this design so I made this insert that allows the use of two M4 x 16mm countersunk head screws.` The designed it to use 4mm heat set inserts. https://a.co/d/0dv4AGsl Finally, I purchased this red dot finder scope https://a.co/d/04XIdzyd My only criticism is that even on the dimmest setting it's still pretty bright. I printed all the parts in ABS at 0.16mm layers, 6 wall loops, 20-25% gyroid infill with 3 fill lines. PETG or either ABS or PETG CF would also be nice, but I didn't have that and the normal ABS seems plenty stiff enough. This print requires minimum supports. I would not print in PLA, as it will warp if left in a hot car. I flocked the inside of the telescope tube and shroud, and painted the inside of the upper tube and spider in Musou black paint. https://a.co/d/06kpUJR0 https://a.co/d/05EYCLqY When assembling the strut rods into the upper tube assembly, it's a snug press fit and might require some persuasion with a plastic tipped hammer. The ends of the tubes must be flush with the bottom of the counter-bores. A keen eye will notice the end screws are missing on my telescope. I lost one somewhere along the way but I made the counter-bores a little too tight and makes installing the screw difficult. I fixed this on the uploaded model. I contacted Celestron and Skywatcher for replacement screws but neither were any help, so I'm on my own to find a suitable substitute but it seems like an odd thread. The tube extension fits into a groove and is fixed in place with CA glue. The shroud snaps in firmly, glue is optional. I used a soldering iron set to 280-290C to set the threaded inserts. All finished I could not be happier with the performance of the 'scope. It focuses fast and easy, especially with the Bahtinov mask. The 10:1 micro adjust is a dream. Collimation is easy and holds solidly. Vibrations are minimal and settle quickly.

Atmos Mk 1.2 The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a compact 3D-printable model rocket designed for use with Estes E16-6 and E16-8 motors . It features a dedicated electronics bay that can fit a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2 , GY-BME280 pressure sensor , and a 3.7V LiPo battery , allowing makers to add custom flight computers, altitude logging, and other experimental electronics. Designed with accessibility and customization in mind, the Atmos Mk 1.2 can be printed using a wide range of common 3D printing materials. Whether printed in PLA for easy prototyping, PETG for added durability, or other materials for specialized builds, the design can be adapted to suit different launch goals. The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a platform for makers, students, and rocketry enthusiasts who want to explore 3D printing, electronics, and experimental flight systems in a compact and reusable rocket design. Flight Notes Stability margin: Approximately 1.7 calibers . Estimated altitude: Typically reaches 800–1,000 ft (240–305 m) , depending on launch conditions. Flight history: Successfully tested over 3 flights (with a 4th planned) with E16-8 estes rocket motors, demonstrating reliable performance and durable construction, you could use f motors but i wouldn't go below 15N of force engines to ensure safe liftoff. Recommendations: do not attempt to remove the motor directly after flight wait for the plastic to cool read assembly note carefully to prevent hardware issues higher temp materials ensure more durability but i have printed out of both pla and petg for this project and pla will function and work I assembled a flight computer out of a raspberry pi pico a gy bme barometer and a small quadcopter battery for under ten dollars and this platform was mostly designed to test it i encourage others to do the same but also i plan to drop links to my functioning code later once i have it all ironed out Assembly Notes To assemble the Atmos Mk 1.2, you'll need 3–4 pennies, super glue, a nylon or Kevlar shock cord, a small amount of duct tape, recovery wadding, a small i hook, and your choice of recovery system (streamer or parachute) . The rocket is designed for Estes E16-6 or E16-8 motors . The nose cone includes a dedicated ballast pocket: Payload under 15 g: Glue 4 pennies into the nose cone. Payload over 15 g: Glue 3 pennies into the nose cone. For the best flight performance, try to keep payloads under 30 g . Secure your electronics using M3 screws, electrical tape, or both —tape alone works well for most builds, but using both provides maximum security. If any printed parts fit loosely, adjust the tolerances with a small amount of Scotch tape as needed. Finally, don't forget to add recovery wadding before every launch. Dozy vive en los Árboles Altos del Oeste, donde avanza tan despacio que a veces tarda un día entero en cambiar de rama. Le gusta tomarse su tiempo, porque dice que los árboles cuentan mejor las cosas cuando nadie los apura. Una mañana empezó a trepar por un tronco cubierto de musgo. Al caer la tarde seguía allí, y justo entonces vio algo que otros no habían notado: a distintas horas del día, la luz iba marcando pequeñas líneas en la corteza, una tras otra, hasta formar la misma curva del camino antiguo. Así entendió una pequeña parte del misterio. Algunas pistas de Zoora no están escondidas por el lugar, sino por el momento: solo aparecen completas cuando se les da el tiempo que necesitan. Desde entonces, Dozy ya no siente que vaya tarde. Ahora sabe que avanzar despacio también puede ayudarte a ver lo que otros pasan por alto. Moraleja: No todo llega tarde por ir lento; a veces ir despacio es justo lo que te permite entenderlo.

Update: keychain versions added on Plate 2 of each print profile! Rainbow trout are a member of the salmon family distinguished by dark green, pink, and white coloration with black spots. Originally native to to the Pacific basin, including eastern Russia, the Aleutian islands, Alaska, western Canada, and the west coast of the United stated, they have been introduced to many other waterways worldwide. In the US in the 1800's a government stocking program started stocking these prized game fish in lakes, rivers, and streams across the country. For this reason, rainbow trout are typically the first trout caught by young anglers (myself included). Rainbow trout come in many forms and subspecies. steelhead are a type that will live out at sea but return to the streams they were born in to spawn. Redbands are subspecies set apart by the vibrant red coloration of their lateral line. Palamino, golden, or banana trout are gold in color but still keep their pink lateral line. This subspecies originated from a single color mutation discovered in a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 that is still propagated to this day. These cold water fish usually weigh between 1-5lbs. This model is the newest edition to my articulated fish collection. Same interlocking scales, same assembly, same swimming motion. To reduce the number of swaps, I've included a non-spotted version to eliminate an additional color change on almost every layer. Just use a thin paintbrush and black acrylic paint to paint the dots on the model after printing. Advantage: less waste, no bleeding of black into white Disadvantage: acrylic paint is water soluble so the dots could be washed off. About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating. description: About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating.
